    ]]>         Video game industry believes EU Kids Act will drive small creators and old games into extinction https://euobserver.com/241743/video-game-industry-believes-eu-kids-act-will-drive-small-creators-and-old-games-into-extinction/ Fri, 09 Oct 2026 07:33:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241743 Campaigners have warned that stringent requirements to adapt games to children by default would prompt the extinction of small games and make costs spiral for developers.]]> A new law aimed at protecting children could kill off old video games and threaten small developers, industry trade groups have warned.

    The EU Kids Act was unveiled by commission president Ursula von der Leyen last month as a chance to “give childhood back to our children” and put parents “in the driving seat”.

    It would require videogames to be catered to children by default with stringent requirements including an eight-hour nighttime lock-out, a ban on screenshots, and guardian supervision.

    Gamers wanting to play the full version of games would have to pass age verification checks to access features, like multi-player tournaments or mystery boxes. 

    The European Commission is gathering feedback on the act with respondents quick to criticise the threat posed to videogame makers.

    Stop Killing Games, a campaign to protect videogames, has opposed the act.

    “This could turn the EU into a pariah state for videogames,” said Ross Scott, the consumer group’s founder. He reckons the regulation could spark a race to update games or deactivate them.

    MEPs have also joined in sounding the alarm bell.

    Proposed law could kill games

    If the law passed, developers would need to make a child mode version of games and gate the full games behind a verification step.

    “This is going to bury developers with compliance steps, and a whole lot of cost,” said Scott.

    Age verification with zero-knowledge proof (meaning developers cannot collect data) will likely be required. “In practice, providers would likely need to engage a third-party age assurance provider,” also said Lauro Fava, partner at law firm Pinsent Masons.

    The Commission’s impact assessment claims that third-party age verification apps would reduce costs, but failed to provide estimates.

    Fava called it “strange” that these were missing, and thinks the commission “arguably downplayed” the cost of compliance.

    Gamer’s Voice, an advocacy group, asserted that small games would struggle to pay for age-verification and other compliance measures, likely to inlclude game redesigns.

    The Kids Act would outlaw features ‘increasing social comparison’ for minors, meaning functions like leaderboards and kill counts could be restricted.

    Read more

    EU plans Europe‑wide social media age limits, but can Brussels really police Big Tech?

    And while the cost to developers is not known, it is feared prices could increase for players.

    The wide scope of the draft law means community servers and hobbyist-developed games could be subjected to the new rules. Any game, new or old, would have to follow measures unless strictly offline in a physical format or built only for educational purposes.

    And since the rules would apply to games made or consumed in the EU, it is feared game makers could block access to their games on the bloc.

    This article continues, but the full version is available only to EUobserver.com subscribers. Visit account.euobserver.com/membership

    ]]>         French kitchenware giant Tefal faces legal ultimatum over harmful chemicals, as Europeans’ health at stake https://euobserver.com/241872/french-kitchenware-tefal-faces-legal-ultimatum-over-harmful-chemicals-as-europeans-health-at-stake/ Fri, 09 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241872 Environmental NGOs have threatened to sue the owner of Tefal, a leading French kitchenware company, over failing to phase out forever chemicals from their products, at a high price for consumer health.]]> Environmental NGOs have threatened to sue the owner of Tefal, a leading French kitchenware company, over failing to phase out forever chemicals from their products, at a high price for consumer health.

    The organisations allege that Groupe SEB, the parent company of known brands, such as Tefal cookware, Calor irons, and Moulinex kitchen appliances, fails to curtail harmful chemicals in its products.

    And the environmentalist groups have threatened to file a lawsuit if the firm fails to makes a change to its policy within three months.

    Companies have a duty to identify and address the impact of their work and products under the French law, for instance the pollution they cause or human rights they might violate.

    Environmental NGOs ClientEarth, Générations Futures and Notre Affaire à Tous say Groupe SEB should swap harmful chemicals in its products to existing alternatives, such as ceramic coating or cast iron, to limit harm to human health and the environment.

    Read more

    Croatia’s toxic waste dump scandal shows the cost of Europe’s ‘forever chemicals’

    The company uses teflon for non-stick, high-temperature suited coatings of their products.

    The substance is one of the ‘PFAS’ polymers, often dubbed forever chemicals, because they break down very slowly, remaining in the environment and human body for a long time. 

    PFAS are widely used for food pots, clothes, packaging, and waterproof products.

    But since they take so long to decompose, they are often found in soil and groundwater. Many of the substances cause cancer, others are harmful to babies in the womb.

    Teflon is allegedly “not absorbed by the human body” and is approved by the World Health Organisation (WHO) for contact with food, the company’s website says.

    Read more

    Sweden moves to ban ‘forever chemicals’ in consumer products from 2028 as EU-wide ban remains in limbo

    However, a recent risk assessment by the EU’s Chemical Agency’s (ECHA), quoted by the NGOs, points out that when overheated or scratched, teflon releases PFAS particles.

    It also releases substances harmful to the environment during the manufacturing process, ECHA’s research found in March.

    And a new European law on the issue will provide a “more consistent basis for corporate due diligence litigation,” Hélène Duguy, ClientEarth’s lawyer in the case, told EUobserver.

    An EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence directive, inspired by French legislation, will oblige all companies based in the EU to address the impact of their operations on the environment and human rights.

    Member states must implement national laws fulfilling the obligation by summer 2028.

    SEB can show stopping PFAS use is “necessary and feasible,” setting a precedent for others, Duguy said.

    Groupe SEB was approached for comment.

    ]]>         EU Parliament’s 7 October memorial honours Israelis, sidelines Palestinians — and sows division https://euobserver.com/241740/eu-parliaments-7-october-memorial-honours-israelis-sidelines-palestinians-and-sows-division/ Thu, 08 Oct 2026 18:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241740 A memorial to victims of 7 October in Israel, which made no mention of Palestinian casualties, ended in tumbling flags, anger, and grief. ]]> An EU Parliament memorial for victims of the 7 October attack caused disarray and anger as well as grief in a divided European house.

    It was crowned by a towering Israeli flag, alongside the EU’s.

    The exhibit set up in Strasbourg’s parliament included maps showing Occupied Palestinian Territories as part of Israel and sold trinkets made from debris of Israeli missiles.

    But it made no mention of the 74,200 people killed by Israel in Gaza in the past three years, after Palestinian militants Hamas killed some 1,200 Israelis in a surprise attack.

    This situation struck a chord with the sole Palestinian in parliament, left-wing French MEP Rima Hassan, who tried to take down the Israeli flag in protest, and toppled over the EU one as well in an unwanted domino effect.

    “My action was in no way directed at the victims of 7 October or their memory,” Hassan told EUobserver. 

    Instead, it targeted “this incessant and untenable double standard, for a Russian flag would never be permitted, and rightly so, within the [EU] institution’s premises”.

    The memorial was organised by German centre-right MEP Hildegard Bentele, who chairs the parliament’s Israel delegations, alongside the Israeli embassy, and the The International Movement for Peace & Coexistence (IMPAC) group in Brussels, as well as others.

    “During a conversation with a member of my team, the guest artist [at the EU Parliament memorial] claimed that Palestine ‘does not exist’,” Hassan added.

    Her family were expelled from their birthplace by Israel in 1948 along with hundreds of thousands of others in what Palestinians call the Nakba (Catastrophe).

    But in the cacophony of narratives in the EU assembly, those who saw her anti-Israel flag protest as offensive or antisemitic had echoing voices.

    ]]>         EU let member states rewrite targets after they had sought recovery-fund payment, auditors find  https://euobserver.com/241815/eu-let-member-states-rewrite-targets-after-they-had-sought-recovery-fund-payment-auditors-find/ Thu, 08 Oct 2026 15:43:58 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241815 The revised targets were "aligned with actual achieved outputs, which made the payment possible," the auditors wrote in their annual report on last year's budget. ]]> EU governments were allowed to water down targets in their post-Covid pandemic recovery plans after they had already asked Brussels for the money, the European Court of Auditors (ECA) said on Thursday (8 October).

    Of 20 milestones and targets the auditors examined, 13 were amended after the member state had already submitted its payment request. In nine of those cases, the change itself was requested after the payment application had already been made. 

    The revised targets were “aligned with actual achieved outputs, which made the payment possible,” the auditors wrote in their annual report on the 2025 EU budget.

    Rewriting measures

    Ireland, for example, asked for a payment in December 2024. But in January 2025 it requested to cut the target for ICT graduates down from 12,450 to 10,900, citing a high administrative burden.

      <title>US’s Reagan-era economic promises return as Trump’s AI-fueled growth fantasy</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/11/trump-ai-economy-reagan</link>
      <description><p>‘Even if AI supercharged the economy, its impact on the government’s finances would be muted’</p><p>Back through political history to the age of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ronald-reagan">Ronald Reagan</a>, Republicans have repeatedly promised the US public that tax cuts would pay for themselves, firing up economic growth and filling the government’s coffers.</p><p>The promise never really panned out. From the Gipper’s day on, the Republicans’ tax cuts inevitably increased the budget deficit. Despite its failure, though, the promise is back, coated in a fine new layer of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/artificialintelligenceai">artificial intelligence</a> pixie dust. It will fail again.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/11/trump-ai-economy-reagan">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Trump establishes committee to investigate Fed governor Lisa Cook</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/09/trump-investigate-lisa-cook-fed-governor</link>
      <description><p>US president renews his efforts to oust Cook despite supreme court ruling that her firing was unconstitutional</p><p>Donald Trump announced on Friday that he is establishing a committee to investigate Lisa Cook, the US Federal Reserve governor, over allegations that she committed mortgage fraud, renewing his efforts to oust her despite <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jun/29/supreme-court-trump-lisa-cook-ruling">a June supreme court ruling</a> that her earlier firing was unconstitutional.</p><p>Trump said a committee will consult with justice department officials to decide whether there is “cause” for her removal.       <description><p>New report on economic cost of anti-immigration campaign projects 8.6% reduction in retirement payments by 2034</p><p>Elderly Americans can expect to lose an average of $2,152 in annual social security benefits each, a projected 8.6% reduction in their retirement payments, by 2034 and every year after as a direct consequence of the economic fallout from the Trump administration’s <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/series/ice-2-0-inside-trumps-new-immigration-dragnet">anti-immigration campaign</a>, if that carries on, according to a new report shared exclusively with the Guardian.</p><p>Already, US food prices are up, housing permits to build new homes are down – and even native-born Americans are losing out on potential jobs after the sudden exodus of 1.2 million foreign-born workers over the last two years as a result of Donald Trump’s policies, the report finds.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/09/trump-immigration-cost-social-security">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/oct/08/trump-media-ban-hearing</link>
      <description><p>Lawyer for CNN, MS Now and Politico says Trump admitted he banned networks from White House over their coverage</p><p>Donald Trump continues to be the strongest witness for the media companies arguing that they were unfairly barred from the White House at his direction, a lawyer representing CNN, MS Now and Politico told a federal judge on Thursday afternoon.</p><p>The media coalition was in court asking the judge to extend the temporary restraining order (TRO) he issued on 24 September requiring the White House to lift the ban for 14 days. That temporary reprieve was scheduled to expire on Thursday, but district court judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, said he would extend it until Tuesday and that he would probably rule on a motion for a preliminary injunction by that day.       <description><p>An initiative on November’s ballot aims to overturn the 9.9% tax on earnings above $1m – who’s winning the fight? </p><p>Voters in Washington state will soon decide the fate of the state’s so-called “<a href="https://senatedemocrats.wa.gov/millionaires-tax-faq/">millionaire tax</a>” – a 9.9% income tax on earnings above $1m that was <a href="https://governor.wa.gov/news/2026/governor-ferguson-signs-millionaires-tax-law">signed</a> into law in March and is now facing a conservative-backed effort to repeal it.</p><p>An <a href="https://leg.wa.gov/media/ucubvqsd/2026-summary-of-initiative-26-645.pdf">initiative</a> on November’s ballot aims to overturn the tax, claiming that the tax represents a slippery slope, and would eventually result in taxes for more than just millionaires.       <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/03/salinas-california-john-steinbeck</link>
      <description><p>John Steinbeck’s hometown of Salinas is the least affordable city in the US for the middle class, a recent Brookings Institution analysis found </p><p>Nestled between two mountain ranges at the crook of central California’s coastline sits a valley known as the “salad bowl of the world”.</p><p>Farm workers stoop over neatly lined rows of crops off Highway 101 to harvest more than half of the nation’s supply of lettuce and nearly a third of its strawberries. The soil here is so rich that author John Steinbeck made the Salinas valley the promised land in his literary depictions of people chasing the American dream: immigrants, farm workers, westward-moving hopefuls, hungering for a better life.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/03/salinas-california-john-steinbeck">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comMon, 12 Oct 2026 10:14:11 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Takeover panel rejects PTSB sale complaints from ex-banker ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/financial-services/2026/10/12/takeover-panel-rejects-ptsb-sale-complaints-from-ex-banker/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/financial-services/2026/10/12/takeover-panel-rejects-ptsb-sale-complaints-from-ex-banker/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 09:48:30 +0000The Irish Takeover Panel has rejected concerns raised about the PTSB sale process from a firm cofounded by boom-time Irish banker Mark Duffy, which has also indicated it is considering an 11th-hour bid for the bank.

Axis Capital, an advisory business cofounded by former Bank of Scotland (Ireland) chief executive Duffy, sent a letter to the panel on July 27th which consolidated “a number of matters” it had previously raised in relation to the proposed €1.62 billion acquisition of PTSB by Austrian banking group Bawag.

The panel said that “having carefully considered the substance of all of the matters raised by Axis”, it has ruled that there is no case laid out that amounted to any breach of Irish takeover rules.

The announcement comes just weeks before the High Court, which is overseeing the so-called scheme of arrangement deal for PTSB to be sold to Bawag, is due to hold its sanctioning hearing on October 27th.

Axis separately made an intervention on October 2nd saying it was considering making a bid for PTSB. Last Friday, a long-term dissenting PTSB shareholder, Scotchstone Capital, led by Piotr Skoczylas, also said it was weighing a bid for PTSB. Neither has confirmed whether it is working with an investment bank, nor whether it has secured any funding for a bid.

Axis helped initiate talks in 2025 between New York private equity firm Centerbridge, the Department of Finance and PTSB over a potential deal for the Irish bank. The US group subsequently submitted a non-binding proposal in September last year for the State’s 57.5 per cent stake in the bank.

Centerbridge would end up as the underbidder to Bawag in April as a formal sales process, initiated in October, concluded.

Axis was reported by the Business Post in July to have been urging minority shareholders to vote against the planned Bawag deal at an extraordinary general meeting (EGM) later that month. Axis said in a note circulated to shareholders that it had become “increasingly uncomfortable with the way the process has developed”, claiming there to have been “inordinate involvement from one shareholder, leaving others effectively as bystanders”.

Duffy said in a post on LinkedIn, the professional social networking platform, in July that the panel should reopen the sale process to allow “all credible bidders to make their best and final bids to all shareholders”.

PTSB secured backing from 91.3 per cent of shareholders – led by the Government – for the Bawag takeover at the July EGM. However, some 36 per cent of minority investors voted against the transaction at the meeting.

It is expected that the High Court will be asked by some minority shareholders to order the holding of a separate vote of minority investors. PTSB has repeatedly said that it has “very strong” legal advice that only one vote is necessary.

]]><![CDATA[AI being used by employers to more closely monitor their staff, Dublin conference hears]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/12/employers-use-ai-to-monitor-staff-who-also-dont-benefit-from-the-tech-conference-hears/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/12/employers-use-ai-to-monitor-staff-who-also-dont-benefit-from-the-tech-conference-hears/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 07:00:00 +0000Artificial intelligence (AI) is being used by employers to more closely monitor their staff to make them more productive, a trade union organised conference in Dublin has heard.

The event was organised by the Communications Workers Union (CWU) in response to what was felt to be a lack of union or civil society voices at this Wednesday’s Government-organised AI Summit in the RDS.

Canadian critic and author Paris Marx told the conference AI technology was often used for surveillance of one type or another on staff, while the quality of work being done by workers was being degraded with consequences for pay.

“What’s happening varies across different sectors,” he said. “We see in graphic design settings and translation settings, it’s not always that people are being actually replaced by AI but often it’s that people who would have done the initial work – and been paid well – are now being relegated to editing an AI-generated piece of translation or image.

“Because they are not the original creator they are being paid a lot less despite the fact that the work can take just as long or longer to do.”

Marx said moves are also afoot in some sectors, such as the legal profession, to “completely eliminate” a lot of entry level roles and work.

He said this was occurring “without much thought for what will happen in 10 to 15 years when the people who would have done that work will be needed to replace more senior lawyers who are retiring”.

“So we need to be concerned not just about the jobs that are being or might be lost but also about the way jobs are changing,” he said.

Who’s hiring and who’s firing in Ireland’s technology sector?

Commenting on the AI-related findings in the Working In Ireland survey, Demitrios Argyros said the results suggested a majority of people using AI at work felt it resulted in them doing more complex or creative work.

A consequence of this, he said, is they felt the parts of their day when they were doing easier tasks or basic admin had been reduced and so their working day had become more intense, leaving them more drained by their day’s work.

AI bubble? Nvidia is now bigger than Japan, but valuation looks modest

“They feel they work more and do higher value work but they are not getting more pay or time off so there is a sense the productivity gains are all going to the employer when they could be shared through shorter hours, reduced workloads or investment on worker development,” he said.

The event was also told State agencies here and public bodies were becoming too dependent on a handful of huge American corporations at a time when Donald Trump has suggested he regards their AI and software products as a tool of his foreign policy.

That tech, Abeba Birhane of Trinity College suggested, was built on what even a Microsoft insider had described as a massive theft of other people’s work.

Patrick Bresnihan, of Maynooth University, said the construction resources employed to build data centres in Ireland since 2019 would have been sufficient to provide 50,000 houses.

Ian McArdle, of the CWU, said: “You cannot have a serious conversation about the future of AI and work without the people who do that work.

“The conference was about ensuring workers have a voice in the shaping of the future of AI rather than simply having to live with the consequences.”

]]>Picture: Finbarr O'Rourke<![CDATA[‘A slow-moving tsunami’: IMF chief alarmed at AI threat to jobs and taxes]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/12/imf-chief-alarmed-at-slow-moving-tsunami-of-ai-for-jobs-taxes/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/12/imf-chief-alarmed-at-slow-moving-tsunami-of-ai-for-jobs-taxes/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 07:49:31 +0000The head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned of the disruptive threat from artificial intelligence to the labour market and taxation, urging policymakers to rethink education and act now to help society adapt.

“It is a slow-moving tsunami, but [a] tsunami nonetheless,” managing director Kristalina Georgieva said Monday during her first appearance at the annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok.

Speaking at a session on artificial intelligence’s (AI’s) impact on employment, she said the technology is already hollowing out demand for many human workers by taking over routine, repetitive tasks. At the same time, it is increasing low-paying jobs in sectors like construction, which she said is “not a story to celebrate”.

It is a transformation with far-reaching consequences for public finances, Georgieva said. The risk is that AI strains government revenues by tilting the economy toward capital and away from labour – traditionally the main source of tax income.

The comments are the latest warning about the potential shock from AI on jobs and the global economy. Young workers in AI-exposed fields have already seen a slowdown in hiring, leaving new entry-level applicants far more vulnerable. Concern is also growing that the technology will widen inequality, with its gains so far concentrated among a narrow set of workers and economies despite a global investment supercycle.

“We cannot today imagine what exactly the world of work will be five years from now,” she said. “But we can be disciplined and carefully assess what is happening, and then draw lessons, but – most importantly – act on them now.”

Despite the employment headwinds, the technology can ultimately prove a positive for growth overall. The IMF estimates the spread of AI can add up to a percentage point to growth in advanced Asian economies.

Such a growth boost “is a very big deal,” Georgieva said, adding it will “more than offset” the drag from ageing in rich countries across the region. – Bloomberg

]]>Heather Diehl<![CDATA[The signs are AI prefers AI-written CVs, and one law firm’s experience is revealing]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/12/what-if-ai-prefers-cvs-written-by-ai/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/12/what-if-ai-prefers-cvs-written-by-ai/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000Earlier this year, in the depths of summer, the Addleshaw Goddard law firm found itself in a slight pickle.

In what was becoming a familiar pattern, an advert it had placed for an IT job in its human resources department had drawn a slew of applications.

A year ago, only a couple of dozen people might have sent in a resume for a position like this one. But AI has made the job of applying for a job much faster and easier, and this time 178 applications arrived.

The problem was, the longer it took to sift them, the higher the chance that good candidates would find work elsewhere. Like a lot of organisations, Addleshaw has been encouraging its managers to test ways that AI can safely improve its processes, so the firm’s HR department decided to do an experiment. It would see how well an AI agent could assess the applications compared with humans.

An agent was duly set up, using the firm’s internal Microsoft Copilot system, and told about the role that needed to be filled, as well as the experience applicants would need with certain HR systems and programming languages, and with AI itself.

Humans at the firm sorted the applicants into a shorter pile of about a dozen and asked the agent to score them.

The agent whipped through this task and presented a list of what it deemed to be the top contenders. The humans did the same thing.

Alas, the two lists did not match. The agent was impressed by glossy applications from candidates who claimed to have achieved exceptional IT feats in record time at a previous employer, or worked on big projects despite scant levels of experience. In short, they were too good to be true – and smacked of having been written with the help of AI.

Who’s hiring and who’s firing in Ireland’s technology sector?

Katherine Rathbone, Addleshaw Goddard’s head of HR, told me her team had theories about why this might have happened.

For one thing, AI tools can make it a lot easier for candidates to tailor a CV to match a job description. But that was not all. “One possible explanation is that, because AI capability was itself one of the criteria, the agent may have interpreted signs of AI use in producing the CV as evidence of AI capability,” she said.

There is another, more disturbing possibility. The AI agent may have actively preferred CVs purely because AI was involved in writing them.

If so, it would confirm the findings of an eye-catching working paper that has analysed the behaviour of AI hiring tools.

The researchers simulated what they said were realistic hiring processes for 24 jobs ranging from teachers and consultants to chefs and engineers. They discovered that candidates using the same AI large language model as the recruiter were between 23 per cent and 60 per cent more likely to be shortlisted than those who relied on CVs produced by a hapless human.

AI bubble? Nvidia is now bigger than Japan, but valuation looks modest

This human handicap was highest for business roles such as sales and accountancy and lowest for fields such as farming and automobiles.

The paper is still being revised for publication in a peer-reviewed journal, meaning some of its findings may change. But one of its authors, Jiannan Xu, told me that updated analyses continue to provide evidence that AI models “exhibit self-preferencing behaviour”.

That is disturbing news at a time when AI is already driving a dismal hiring arms race. On one side are job hopefuls who, convinced they are battling a wall of soulless recruitment tools, are fighting back with an explosion of AI applications that are swamping recruiters.

If AI is biased towards AI, it adds a fresh dimension of jeopardy. Imagine being the candidate using the wrong type of AI, or no AI at all.

Fortunately, Xu’s paper suggests AI bias can be more than halved with two relatively simple strategies: telling models to ignore the origin of résumés and focus on their content, and using a number of assessment models to dilute the bias of any single tool.

Meanwhile at Addleshaw Goddard, I was pleased to learn that the successful candidate for the IT job was chosen by humans, and was not the one the agent ranked highest.

And as for using AI for recruitment, it is still a work in progress. The tools clearly have potential if used correctly, says Rathbone. “But human judgment remains important. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

]]>Kanawa_Studio<![CDATA[Irish AI firms raise €256m across 75 venture capital deals in 2026]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/irish-ai-firms-raise-256m-across-75-venture-capital-deals-in-2026/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/irish-ai-firms-raise-256m-across-75-venture-capital-deals-in-2026/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000Irish artificial intelligence (AI) companies continue to attract near-record levels of funding from venture capital firms, despite a fall-off in the value and volume of deals in 2026 compared to last year.

New research from Pitchbook, the global private capital markets intelligence firm, found that companies in the Republic’s AI sector have raised an additional €256 million across 75 deals so far this year.

The 2026 figures represent a decline from the record €691.3 million across 107 deals in 2025, the firm said.

It meant that the median deal value has fallen to €1.6 million in 2026 compared with €2.4 million last year. However, this is still above the median for any year before 2025.

Pitchbook said in the report that after a blockbuster year in 2025, the drop-off in 2026 reflects “normalisation rather than retreat”. It said the market was “settling after a banner year for investment” in 2025, in which several large-scale deals exceeding €100 million each were recorded.

The 2025 total includes, for example, Wayflyer’s €161.8 million fundraising round and workflow software platform Tines’ €120.7 million Series C round.

Highlights of 2026 so far include Fonoa’s €94.1 million fundraise to expand its tax compliance automation capabilities. Meanwhile, CameraMatics raised €49 million for its vehicle safety and fleet management software.

Enterprise Ireland, which says it has participated in 392 Irish AI funding rounds since 2020 in nearly two-thirds of Irish AI deals in 2026 to date, published the research on Monday morning in advance of the International AI Summit in Dublin on October 14th.

AI bubble? Nvidia is now bigger than Japan, but valuation looks modest

The event, which is part of the Republic’s presidency of the EU Council, takes place at the RDS in Ballsbridge, Dublin 4.

“PitchBook’s independent analysis shows the scale of investment now going into Irish AI companies, with almost €1 billion raised since the beginning of 2025,” said Jenny Melia, chief executive of Enterprise Ireland.

“The level of investment reflects the calibre and growing maturity of Irish AI companies, the breadth of sectors they are operating in and the strength of the intellectual property being developed in Ireland.”

Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence Niamh Smyth said: “The International AI Summit will focus on how Europe can turn advances in AI into economic value, while building the skills, infrastructure and trusted regulatory environment needed to support adoption and investment.”

Global M&A and fundraising activity has been mixed so far this year. While deals worth a record $2.8 trillion (€2.5 trillion) were agreed in the first half of the year, according to recent data from the London Stock Exchange group, European transaction volumes tumbled 14.2 per cent as the region faced an outsize impact from the Iran war.

]]>Orla Murray/Coalesce<![CDATA[Frantic behind-the-scenes talks delivers deal on EU capital markets reform]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/frantic-behind-the-scenes-talks-delivers-deal-on-eu-capital-markets-reform/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/frantic-behind-the-scenes-talks-delivers-deal-on-eu-capital-markets-reform/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000When the EU’s finance ministers sat down for a working dinner in Luxembourg last Thursday evening, Simon Harris warned his counterparts they could be about to face another day of newspaper headlines bashing Europe for again ducking a big decision.

Or, they could strike a deal, even if the compromise on the table wasn’t perfect, the Irish Minister for Finance said.

Finance officials had been toiling for months over a contentious package of reforms intended to break a decade long logjam. The proposals would shift more responsibility for regulating the architecture that makes the financial markets tick from national central banks and authorities to a European regulator.

Simplifying this layer of oversight would hopefully make it easier for investment cash and funding to flow across national borders, ideally creating a bigger pool of European capital that businesses could tap to raise investment and expand.

The Irish Government had set itself a tight deadline when taking over the Council of the EU presidency in July. It wanted to agree a deal on the hugely technical package of financial legislation by the October meeting of EU finance ministers.

Harris, who would be chairing discussions during the EU presidency, had gone back and forth with his advisers about tying himself to a firm date. Ultimately they decided it would help put the pressure on everyone.

The Council of the EU is the body where the member states, either at the level of officials, ambassadors, or ministers, shape policy coming from Brussels. The “presidency” rotates from country to country every six months, and for that period you are expected to be a neutral broker, steering the debate towards a common compromise.

Political agreement had long proved elusive when it came to reforms of the EU’s capital markets.

EU governments agree on long-stalled capital markets reform

The idea has been knocking around for a long time – a very long time in fact.

“Though a European capital market ought to be the result of spontaneous developments, it will nonetheless require constructive efforts on the part of governments and financial institutions,” Italian economist Claudio Segré wrote in a 1966 report for the then-European Economic Community (ECC).

An expert group chaired by Segré, a commission official, said creating a “broad” European capital market made good economic sense.

Brussels officials took a proper stab at it in the years that followed the financial crash.

Jean-Claude Juncker, then-European Commission president, spoke about creating a “capital markets union” in 2014. The changes would involve greater regulation at EU rather than national level, and aligning things such as insolvency regimes and other financial rules.

Building on banking reforms in the post-crash period, the president of the EU’s lawmaking body said the changes would “increase the attractiveness of Europe as a place to invest”.

Ireland’s EU presidency proposes budget cut of €141bn for the bloc

Everyone agrees in principle, but individual national capitals had traditionally been nervous that they would lose out in the shake-up.

France has been a big fan of the plan. That’s no surprise given the reforms would expand the remit of the existing European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), which is based in Paris.

Ireland and Luxembourg, two small member states with big financial services sectors, eyed plans to hand extra powers over to a European regulator with great suspicion.

The pair had teamed up in the past to oppose a shift towards a souped-up European regulator, fearing companies and firms would be tempted to set up shop in Paris in the future, rather than Dublin or Luxembourg.

Concerns about Europe’s sluggish economy, and a creeping sense the EU was falling further behind the United States and China, reignited the debate.

A 2024 report by another Italian economist, Mario Draghi, said the EU needed to push through the long-stalled capital market reforms to jump-start growth. The former European Central Bank chief warned the alternative would be a slow, painful economic decline.

EU’s big six push to centralise financial oversight in move that will worry Ireland

Breaking down national barriers that were stopping capital and investment from flowing throughout the 27-state union was key to that, Draghi said.

Ursula von der Leyen rebranded the capital reforms the “savings and investment union”, part of which would significantly expand ESMA’s remit to oversee financial markets.

The sprawling piece of complex legislation, the Market Integration and Supervision Package was kicked on to the member states, to see if they could land a deal everyone could live with this time.

Securing that deal by a self-imposed October deadline was ambitious but doable, Harris wrote in a letter to his fellow finance ministers after a meeting in July.

There was broad support around the room to get the thing done, subject to the shape of compromise.

A huge amount of the heavy lifting took place in Brussels at official-level.

A working group, chaired by Irish finance attache Emma Moyles, met more than a dozen times in the following months to knead out the sticky details. Department of Finance colleagues in Dublin were heavily involved too.

Irish negotiators got an honest sense of the red lines and the space for a “landing zone” in separate one-to-one discussions with officials from each of the other member states.

When talking to fellow finance ministers, Harris often mentioned Ireland didn’t need unanimous support to approve a deal, only a qualified majority of EU states, a much easier bar to clear.

A compromise text was drafted and redrafted by the Irish presidency that ran to several hundred pages.

The reworked proposal, seen by The Irish Times, included several big changes aimed at bringing reluctant countries around.

The confidential text shows Luxembourg secured leeway in the oversight of asset management groups. Malta opposed ESMA taking over the regulation of crypto platforms, so European oversight was limited to large platforms.

More broadly, representatives of national authorities and central banks would retain a role in ESMA’s governance too.

It was the carveout to accommodate the Germans that kicked off the biggest storm.

We have achieved more in the last 10 months than we have achieved in the last 10 years

Eelco Heinen, Dutch finance minister

Deutsche Börse Group, who run the Frankfurt Stock Exchange, would not come under the supervision of the EU-level authority, but remain regulated locally.

The German government argued the carveout was justified on the basis Deutsche Börse only operates in Germany, rather than across EU borders. BME, who run the Spanish Stock Exchange, were also exempt from ESMA oversight, following lobbying by Madrid.

Several member states, and the commission, were unhappy with the way Germany bagged an opt-out for its stock exchange, while others were being pressed to hand over decision-making authority to a European supervisor. “If we are doing this, we have to do it altogether,” said a diplomat from one country annoyed at the German carveout.

“If it’s a German sausage at the end of all this, what’s the point of it,” one industry source remarked, a reference to the ugly business of policymaking.

Belgium complained about the need to have a “level playing field”. The Belgian government had unsuccessfully pushed for Euroclear, a major central securities depository in its back yard, to remain regulated at national level.

Ambassadors from each member state, who are their governments’ eyes and ears in Brussels, picked up the debate last Wednesday.

Several sources briefed on the closed-door discussion said about 10 member states intervened to register their annoyance. The European Commission were also frustrated the ambition of the reforms had been “significantly” watered down.

Harris wants deal on contentious EU capital market reforms by October

Officials continued to negotiate deep in the weeds of the massively technical package of reforms, as finance ministers made their way to Luxembourg for their October 9th meeting.

A dinner had been arranged the evening before, where Harris again made the case. They could all spend another six months debating the finer points and they’d probably be in the same position, he said. “No compromise is perfect,” he told the room.

By breakfast the following morning, it seemed clear the other ministers agreed. Word filtered out shortly after they took their seats for the actual EU council meeting: deal done.

“We have achieved more in the last 10 months than we have achieved in the last 10 years,” Dutch finance minister Eelco Heinen later said.

All member states – bar Belgium who abstained – voted to back the compromise crafted by the Irish presidency, faults, carveouts and all.

That’s not the end of things though. MEPs in the European Parliament will have a chance to amend the package, before national governments give their final sign-off.

Speaking at a press conference afterwards, Harris cautioned against waiting around and letting the perfect become the enemy of the good. “That’s not how the European Union works,” he said.

]]>AILBE PHOTO<![CDATA[Budget reversal of policy on tackling climate change was a mistake]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/12/budget-reversal-of-the-policy-on-tackling-climate-change-was-a-mistake/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/12/budget-reversal-of-the-policy-on-tackling-climate-change-was-a-mistake/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000There are three crucial tasks for any budget: does it implement a long-term economic strategy; is the trajectory of the public finances sustainable; and will it manage aggregate demand in the economy so that economic activity remains close to capacity?

]]>MilosStankovic<![CDATA[Ireland goes Swedish on investment, but deemed disposal remains a problem]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/12/ireland-goes-swedish-on-investment-but-deemed-disposal-remains-a-problem/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/12/ireland-goes-swedish-on-investment-but-deemed-disposal-remains-a-problem/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 03:01:00 +0000Earlier this year, Stocktake suggested Minister for Finance Simon Harris might be tempted to borrow Sweden’s model for encouraging people to invest.

Investors can put up to €12,000 a year into the account, with the first €50,000 of investments exempt from tax, while amounts above that will face an annual 1 per cent charge.

Some will be irked by that charge, especially in years where stock markets have fallen. However, a UK-style tax-free wrapper, allowing savers to invest up to £20,000 a year completely free of tax, always appeared excessively generous and politically indefensible.

For the Government, a Swedish-type approach offers a predictable tax stream while encouraging people to put their savings into shares and funds (and a €50,000 tax-free limit is more generous than many expected) rather than leaving them in cash.

However, the new account also highlights the problem with the system outside it. Investments held in the SIA will escape deemed disposal, while investors buying ordinary ETFs will continue to face an eight-year tax charge on unrealised gains, albeit at the reduced rate of 35 per cent.

The Government says it intends to move beyond deemed disposal during the lifetime of this administration, but substantive reform has again been deferred.

And there is a second, less discussed problem. The Funds Sector 2030 review recommended limited loss relief, but the Government’s roadmap says it will not be introduced. As Stocktake previously noted, an investor who makes €5,000 on one ETF and loses €5,000 on another can therefore have no overall gain but still face tax on the €5,000 profit.

Is the State’s new investment account going to be a good deal?

That is less of an issue for someone holding one broad global ETF, but it matters for a portfolio of separate funds.

Some will have issues with the SIA, but it’s arguably a welcome attempt to make investing simpler. The harder task is making the wider investing tax system equally sensible.

In fact, if there was to be reform of the system, it was expected it would address the reality for many looking to buy in or close to Dublin and other big urban centres – that the €500,000 cap on the value of property purchases under the scheme locks out many aspiring first-time buyers.

As one reader put it: “The scheme remains redundant to majority of buyers in Dublin, commuter towns and other cities across the country. The extra €5k does not unlock any new homes or help affordability.” Of course, that was what it was intended to do in the first place.

There is certainly a broader policy debate on whether housing incentive schemes, such as Help to Buy, which were always designed to help developers as much or more than buyers, are an effective use of government funds to ease a housing crisis but we’ll not get into that here.

Your concerns are much more practical. You are in the process and, clearly, this extra €5,000 would be beneficial to you if you are able to claim it.

So what happens to applications that are “in the system”? Do they get assessed under the new rules? Can they be withdrawn and a new application made? And what effect, if any, might that have on your home purchase?

You are not alone. Aideen was also in touch with our Q&A, wanting to know whether she would need to reapply given they have not closed on their home.

And Michelle, who is using the relief, to build her own home and has been approved for the “old” €30,000 relief but has not yet claimed the money has much the same query.

Mairéad is further along in the process, having already received €30,000 under the scheme. Is she now entitled to this additional €5,000 in relief, she wonders.

For Mairéad, the answer, unsurprisingly, is “no”. If you have already got your money, as with any other tax and relief headings, your application was assessed under rules in place at the time and you cannot benefit (or suffer) from changes in the rules subsequent to receiving your benefit.

Revenue confirmed for me that the new rules kick in on October 7th, the day after the budget. That follows the passing of financial resolution on the budget change to the scheme in the Oireachtas.

Who is eligible? Anyone who has either not signed a contract to buy their home before October 7th or, in the case of those building their own homes, has not yet drawn down the first tranche of their approved mortgage loan.

Revenue notes that some taxpayers may have submitted an application to see if they are eligible or to find out the amount they are eligible to claim under Help to Buy.

“The test to be applied, however, is whether they have signed a contract to purchase a qualifying property or made the first draw down of a mortgage (in the case of a self-build qualifying property),” they tell me.

Minister rules out raising cap on Help-to-Buy scheme for homes worth over €500k

So if you signed the contract with the developer to buy your home before last Wednesday (October 7th) or, for self-build projects, had drawn down any of your mortgage before that date, you will not benefit from the new, higher tax relief threshold.

In your case, although you have not yet drawn down any funds under the relief, you say you have signed the contracts – albeit you are waiting for them to come back from the builder’s side, so it appears you will not benefit from the budget measure and will be able to draw down a maximum of €30,000 in tax relief, not €35,000.

Aideen, who says she has not closed on her home, may be eligible as long as she has not signed the purchase contract. Similarly, Michelle, who is building her own place – or having it built for her – may be eligible if she has not drawn down any of her mortgage.

In her case, it does not matter whether she has actually taken ownership of the Help to Buy relief but whether she has tapped her mortgage on the property.

In those cases, where approval had been granted but not activated by any contract or draw down, I expect you will certainly have to reapply as Revenue will have completed the application paperwork.

What is not so clear is what happens for people who have applied to the scheme but have yet to receive Revenue confirmation that they have been accepted. It would make sense that Revenue would apply the new limits to cases in the system but they have not yet confirmed that for me.

Risk

You do raise an interesting related point which, though it appears is not relevant for you at this point, might be for others earlier in the process who are considering reapplying for the scheme to benefit under new rules – what is the risk in doing so?

With demand still exceeding supply, there is always a danger that any delay in the process could see the other side move on to another buyer.

If contracts are in place, everyone is bound by them – and you lose out on the €5,000 – but if there are no contracts yet in place, there is nothing to stop the developer moving on to another buyer rather than waiting for someone to reapply for Help to Buy under new rules – or raise the price of the property.

That’s not to say they will but there is certainly a risk that they might.

Scheme rules

For those looking to apply now for Help to Buy, what do the changes mean.

Essentially, Help to Buy allows you to claim back income tax and deposit interest retention tax (Dirt) you have paid over the four tax years before the one in which you are making the application to help pull together the deposit you need to buy your first home.

All parties to the purchase must be first time buyers and the property must be newly-build, not second-hand. The property cannot be valued at anything above €500,000 and you must also be taking out a mortgage that covers at least 70 per cent of the price of the property.

The maximum you can claim under the new rules is €35,000 or 10 per cent of the property price, whichever is the lower. Before the budget, the figure was €30,000; all other Ts & Cs were the same.

That €35,000 is the relief that applies to the property, not to the individual, so if two of you are buying, you cannot double up the relief to secure €70,000.

The contractor or developer selling you the property must also be on an approved Revenue list which you can find here. That means they have registered under the scheme and, more important from the Revenue perspective, are compliant with taxes.

To be fair, it would be exceptionally unusual for a developer building new homes not to be on the list but it is always worth checking.

Finally, if you do not live in the property for at least five years, you will face a clawback from Revenue of some of the relief granted.

The scheme has been extended – both in scope and deadline – several times since it was first introduced in 2016. As of now, it is scheduled to run until December 31st, 2029.

]]><![CDATA[A good night’s sleep is a class issue]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/11/a-good-nights-sleep-is-a-class-issue/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/11/a-good-nights-sleep-is-a-class-issue/Sun, 11 Oct 2026 09:00:00 +0000In the 1920s, a pair of sociologists set out to study “the interwoven trends that are the life of a small American city” at a time of rapid change.

In their subsequent book about Muncie, Indiana (which they anonymised as “Middletown”), they wrote that the community was divided by time as well as class.

At 6am, the lights were going on in working-class households because their jobs generally began between 6.15 and 7.30am (when they weren’t on night shifts), while the “business class” households remained slumbering until later.

These different working rhythms became political in 1925 when a deadlock emerged over whether the city should adopt “daylight saving time”, which would mean longer light on summer evenings.

The working-class early risers argued they would lose sleep, while the businessmen urged the change “because of golf” and the need to deal with businesses on the east coast.

The competing demands for leisure and business on the one hand, and of our body clocks on the other, have not gone away over the ensuing century. But scientists have learned a lot more about what happens to our health when we prioritise the former over the latter.

In short: nothing good. Many researchers now agree that daylight saving time can interfere with our circadian rhythms. But there are much more dangerous ways to meddle with our biological clocks, the worst of which is to work at night.

It is a myth that night-shift workers can become nocturnal over time. According to the book Life Time by professor of circadian neuroscience Russell Foster, studies suggest that 97 per cent of night shift workers remain synchronised to daytime, which means they have to sleep when their bodies are primed to be awake, and vice versa.

There are consequences for blood pressure and the immune system. The correlations with cancer are so clear that night work has been classed as “probably carcinogenic to humans” by the World Health Organisation’s International Agency for Research on Cancer.

Maynooth-led sleep research will examine links with mental health

Even if you don’t work overnight, evidence suggests that just working against your “chronotype” can be bad for your health. One recent study from Finland looked at what happened to people who gave information about whether they were morning people or “night owls” in 2012 when they were in their mid-40s.

Over the following 12 years, those with evening chronotypes were more likely to end up on disability pensions, even after adjusting for socio-economic factors. One possibility, according to the researchers, is that “traditional working times interfere significantly with the sleeping preferences of late chronotypes, leading to social jet lag”.

But while the prevalence of night work has declined gradually in the US since Middletown was written, there is still a class divide when it comes to work that tramples over your body clock. According to research published this year, most US night workers have no more than a high-school education.

More broadly, the pandemic-induced shift towards remote work has been a bigger boon for white-collar workers (who already had more flexibility over their hours) than anyone else.

What ‘smart’ watches get wrong and right when tracking the quality of your sleep

In Europe, for example, managers have the highest levels of autonomy according to 2024’s vast European Working Conditions Survey, with 40 per cent able to adapt their working hours within certain limits, and 19 per cent having full control over their schedules. In contrast, workers at the bottom end of the pay scale continue to have little control: nearly 80 per cent have schedules set entirely by their employers.

It is possible that advances in automation will eventually do away with the need for humans to work against their body clocks. Already, some logistics companies are beginning to experiment with “lights-out night shifts” in which robots work overnight alone, setting aside those orders that require human assistance until the morning shift arrives.

Self-driving trucks, meanwhile, could cover long highway stretches overnight, saving the “final mile deliveries” for human drivers to do in daytime.

Such a transition would be economically challenging for workers – not least since night-shift work usually pays a premium – but could have huge benefits for human health. It would require careful navigation by policymakers with an eye on science, inequality and the future.

Yet US president Donald Trump sounds much more like a voice from the past. His latest intervention into the “politics of time” is to push for daylight saving time to be made permanent, arguing that it would be good for people who would “like to play golf a little bit without having to run home after 14 holes”. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

No longer – Nvidia now accounts for 5.2 per cent of the MSCI All Country World Index, slightly more than Japan and more than every country except the US.

A casual observer might think this screams AI bubble, but Nvidia is not an obviously expensive stock. It trades on about 15 times estimated earnings, according to market data from Finviz, making it cheaper than 295 of the S&P 500’s component stocks.

The company, too, is acting as if shares are reasonably priced. A fortnight ago, Nvidia authorised an additional $150 billion share buyback, the largest such authorisation in history.

The record-breaking numbers make for an odd combination, with Nvidia simultaneously looking enormous enough to distort global equity indices, whilst remaining relatively inexpensive against the earnings it is producing.

]]>Andy Rain<![CDATA[We have just seen a perfect example of Ireland’s fiscal incontinence]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/10/10/david-mcwilliams-we-have-just-seen-a-perfect-example-of-irelands-fiscal-incontinence/https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/10/10/david-mcwilliams-we-have-just-seen-a-perfect-example-of-irelands-fiscal-incontinence/Sat, 10 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000Nothing focuses the mind like a hanging,” noted Samuel Johnson, according to his biographer James Boswell. The condemned man, realising that he has only a few weeks to live, focuses on what is truly important. The economic equivalent of this expression is: “Nothing focuses the mind like a hard budget.” Hard budgets make countries and organisations efficient, innovative, thoughtful and, by injecting financial discipline, ensure that decision-makers work through their options to get value for money. The hard budget in itself leads to better management, getting more from less, which requires more effort.

In contrast, a sloppy, bloated budget where money is not a problem will lead to waste, cynicism, cutting corners and the abandonment of accounting discipline. When money is wasted, the essential connection between the cost of something and the delivery of quality breaks down.

Without a hard budget, management becomes almost impossible and the corporation, organisation or country drifts, becoming gradually unable to deal with any shocks to the system that might lie ahead. Like someone who allows themselves to get out of shape, their muscles to weaken, and their weight to soar, the person becomes more susceptible to physical and potential emotional or psychological fragility.

Countries and corporations operate in a similar fashion. If they become addicted to easy money, particularly if that money is someone else’s, a gap opens up between reality and fantasy. The managers begin to feel that the money is theirs and they are entitled to it, creating a dependency. Successful management no longer revolves around the best use of the resources to achieve a specific outcome, but rather it becomes a smash-and-grab exercise centred on how much of the “easy” money the managers can get their hands on.

Without a budget constraint, the objective of management becomes size, not efficiency. The organisation becomes an extractive machine, extracting money from the central budget and, as that part of the organisation gets bigger, the fact of its expanding size means that it gobbles up more and more money, needing more every year just to stay still.

This is what has happened to the Irish State. It is a monstrously bloated organisation that has lost all sense of value for money and exists to gorge on cheap, endless cash that is cascading into the coffers from the US multinationals.

In development economics this process, whereby the State becomes hollowed out by too much rather than too little money, is termed the ”resource curse”. When an underdeveloped country without proper institutions finds a resource like oil, money flows in and it is often wasted, ending up in the pockets of the rulers, driving up costs for everyone else. The country ends up unbalanced – rich in parts but without the public infrastructure that the financial windfall could have paid for. Think Nigeria, Angola or Venezuela, where huge oil finds have not elevated the position of the citizens who own the natural resources of the country.

If these countries are synonymous with bad management, the exemplar of good behaviour is Norway, where the oil windfall has been invested judiciously and democratically for future generations, rather than blown on goodies for today.

Now look at Ireland’s equivalent of an oil find – the gusher that is the US multinational money, a spigot of cashflow, the product of clever tax arbitrage, which is flowing into the system to be pilfered by public sector management in a country that can’t even build a proper national rail system.

This week’s budget is a perfect example of the fiscal incontinence that a soft budget generates. First the Government flatters to deceive by announcing an overall surplus of about €9 billion next year. This looks great, but when you consider that the Department of Finance regards about €23 billion of the €34 billion in projected corporation taxes received this year as being transient, then we are in a different world. If we were to strip that out, our underlying surplus becomes a significant deficit of €13 billion to €14 billion for 2027; and, given commitments outlined in this budget, that deficit will widen to about €20 billion by 2029.

Even from a cyclical perspective, a country at full employment does not need any more money thrown at it – the economy is already bursting at the seams – and yet this week’s Budget 2027 is throwing a net €7.4 billion extra into an already bloated system.

New public spending efficiency taskforce to be established within three months

The Government presents it as cost-of-living relief. But the cost of living has risen because prices have risen. Throwing extra money at this problem will not cause prices to fall, but will cause them to rise, while the extra handout to soften the blow will simply increase dependency on handouts rather than cut prices and permanently. So you get the worst of all worlds: handouts which drive prices higher that are mistakenly put forward as a solution to high prices.

The Irish Fiscal Advisory Council’s analysis says spending is growing at double the pace of the Government’s own 5 per cent sustainable limit. Basically, our windfall is being spent rather than saved.

The lack of a hard budget also means that tough decisions are not taken, not just in the area of financial management but in organisational management too. Take, for example, this rotating taoiseach codology. With two bosses – one on the way out, the other on the way in – the lad on the way in is more important for tomorrow, undermining the lad in situ today.

Such management structure means that the incentive for all senior public servants and politicians is to curry favour with the next guy, not the guy in charge, thus undermining the guy in charge.

And by splitting the Department of Finance in two, with the Department of Finance and the Department of Public Expenditure, what’s the aim? Rather than have one department looking after the money, we now have two departments – and, critically, the Department of the Taoiseach, which used to be the nerve centre of final decision making, is now neutered because no one knows which taoiseach is more important: the incumbent or the next guy.

All the while global financial markets, the font of the windfall money that finances the large US tech companies, are becoming more and more nervous about the future.

   <title>Russland greift weiter Energieanlagen an</title>
   <description>Trotz einer von US-Präsident Donald Trump verkündeten „Energiewaffenruhe“ zwischen Kiew und Moskau hat Russland nach Angaben des ukrainischen Präsidenten Wolodymyr Selenskyj Energieanlagen in der Ukraine angegriffen. Die EU äußerste sich am Montag in Sachen „Energiewaffenruhe“ skeptisch und beschloss neue Sanktionen gegen Russland.</description>

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3442796/">
   <title>Simbabwes „Krokodil“ schnappt nach Macht</title>
   <description>Hunger und Armut will Simbabwes Präsident Emmerson Mnangagwa nachhaltig bekämpfen. Wohlstand bis 2030 lautet seine Vision, die auch die am Montag startende Konferenz der Regierungspartei ZANU-PF prägen wird. Doch die von ihm angestrebte wirtschaftliche Öffnung, die etwa die Landrückgabe an einige weiße Bauern umfasst, wird innenpolitisch von einer kontroversen Verfassungsreform begleitet. Kritikerinnen und Kritiker werfen dem als „Krokodil“ bekannten Mnangagwa vor, seine Macht zunehmend absichern zu wollen.</description>

   <description>US-Präsident Donald Trump, der vor den Midterm-Wahlen wegen hoher Spritpreise unter Druck steht, hat am Wochenende diesen auf die Ukraine erhöht. Łukasz Gibała, an independent, has won the mayoral election in Kraków, Poland’s second-biggest city, beating Monika Piątkowska, the candidate backed by Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

With all votes counted by just after 1 a.m. on Monday morning, Gibała had 62.1% against 37.9% for Piątkowska, who had already conceded defeat shortly after 9 p.m. on Sunday night, when exit polls showed a large margin of victory for her opponent. Turnout was 44.3%.

“Today in Poland, more and more people realise that we don’t have to live in the reality that politicians in Warsaw project upon us,” declared Gibała as it became clear he had won. “More and more people realise that we, in our own towns and cities, know better what’s good for us than they do in Warsaw.”

The victory marks a blow for Tusk – whose Civic Coalition (KO) party has its strongest support in large cities – just a year before he seeks to win another term at parliamentary elections. The prime minister had visited Kraków to campaign alongside Piątkowska.

Dziś 11 października 2026 roku, po 24 latach, mieszkańcy odzyskali swoje miasto. Chciałbym podziękować wszystkim Krakowianom, którzy mi zaufali i zdecydowali się oddać ma mnie głos.

To nasze wspólne zwycięstwo. Dziękuję mojej partnerce Adzie, sztabowi i współpracownikom ze… pic.twitter.com/0FsNYwjPkj

— Łukasz Gibała (@LukaszGibala) October 11, 2026

For Gibała, a wealthy businessman who has largely funded his own political career, this was victory at the fourth attempt, having stood in every mayoral contest since 2014, obtaining a growing share of the vote each time.

He stood as an independent, promising to sort out the city’s finances, end cronyism in the appointment of municipal officials, improve public transport and reverse ticket-price increases, and hold a referendum on Kraków’s controversial clean transport zone for vehicles.

He also pledged to favour residents over developers in planning decisions and to counteract the negative effects of tourism in what is Poland’s most-visited city, including by restricting short-term-rental properties.

Gibała’s victory had been expected after he came top in the first round two weeks ago with 36.4% of the vote among the seven candidates who stood. Piątkowska trailed on 29.9%. The top two candidates then met in today’s run-off.

 

Piątkowska was the joint candidate of Tusk’s centrist KO party and the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), which are both part of the national government.

The case involves two Bangladeshi nationals and one Indian, all legal residents in Poland. The incident came to light in December 2025, after witnesses reported seeing the trio leading a goat through the centre of the city of Wałbrzych, before taking it to the back of a kebab bar.

After killing the animal, the men began butchering it for meat, which they were still portioning out when the police arrived. They told officers that the meat was intended for their own consumption. The kebab bar was closed for renovations at the time.

The men also said that such slaughter was customary in their home countries and they were unaware that, with limited exceptions, animals in Poland may generally be slaughtered only at authorised slaughterhouses, reports broadcaster RMF

 

A spokesman for prosecutors, Mariusz Pindera, told the Wirtualna Polska news website that the men’s unfamiliarity with Polish law did not “absolve them of the obligation to comply with the regulations”.

Prosecutors have therefore asked the court for a so-called conditional discontinuation of the case, a very common procedure under Polish law. Almost 25,000 such motions were submitted last year by prosecutors, citing the low social harm of the offences involved, reports Wirtualna Polska.

The court must now decide whether to accept or reject the prosecution’s motion. In the latter case, prosecutors would be required to proceed with an indictment against the suspects and seek a conviction. No hearing date on the motion has yet been set.

A sign installed to warn the public about damage caused by beavers has been destroyed by the beavers themselves, according to the Polish foresters who erected it.

The incident was reported in a post on social media by the forestry district of Lubliniec in southern Poland, which shared photos of the sign, which read “Warning! Damage caused by beavers”. The wooden post it was displayed on had been destroyed in an apparent beaver attack.

“We wanted to warn you about the potential consequences of beaver activity at the pond and the surrounding area – since beavers dig burrows under the road and fell trees near the pond – but the beavers didn’t want you to be warned, so…they cut down the oak post displaying the hazard notice,” wrote the foresters.

“So, if you are around the pond, please exercise caution; and if you spot a piece of wood sticking out of the ground that has been gnawed by beavers, just imagine there was a sign there reading ‘Warning! Damage caused by beavers’.”

Beavers were once almost hunted to extinction in Poland. By 1928, it was estimated that only 235 remained in the country. However, thanks to postwar efforts to reintroduce the animals into the Polish wilderness, the beaver population has grown and is currently estimated at around 150,000.

Ecologists note that beavers play an important role in tackling drought by retaining water through the dams they build. Those dams also create “oases of biodiversity”, notes the state water agency PGW WP.

However, the rodents can cause damage to roads, houses and farmland, which has led some to call for culls to keep beaver numbers down.

The Warsaw region, which includes Poland’s capital and its suburbs, had the highest employment rate in the European Union last year, according to new Eurostat data.

The employment rate among people aged 20-64 in the region stood at 86.9%, more than 10 percentage points above the figure for the EU as a whole. It was also the highest recorded for Warsaw since data began to be collected in 2013.

Last year, only four EU regions had employment rates of at least 85%. Warsaw was followed by Prague in the Czech Republic at 86%, Finland’s Åland Islands at 85.5%, and Utrecht in the Netherlands at 85.4%.

The EU average stood at 76.1%, slightly below the target of 78% the bloc set for itself for 2030.

At the other end of the scale, 64 of the EU’s 244 regions had employment rates below 74% last year. The lowest was recorded in France’s overseas departments of Mayotte (36.9%) and French Guiana (50%), followed by Italy’s Calabria (50.3%), Campania (50.8%) and Sicily (51.4%).

After Warsaw, the second-highest employment rate in Poland was recorded in the central Łódź province (80.8%) while the lowest was in the southeastern Subcarpathian province (73.2%). The figure for the country as a whole was 78.8%, which was only the 13th highest in the EU.

In addition to topping the overall employment rate ranking, Warsaw also had the third lowest rate of youth employment (for people aged 15-29) at 3.9%, higher only than Yugozapaden in Bulgaria (3.8%) and Zeeland in the Netherlands (3.6%).

And it had the third-highest rate of employment among people with tertiary education (93.5%), behind only Portugal’s Região Autónoma dos Açores (94.6%) and Yugozapaden (93.6%).

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 7, 2025

The most recent Eurostat figures, from August, show that Poland’s unemployment rate (3.3%) was the second-lowest among all member states and well below the EU-wide figure of 6.2%.

The strong labour market reflects years of economic growth, rising wages and increased employment. However, Poland’s ageing and shrinking population is creating labour shortages and encouraging companies to invest more heavily in automation.

At the same time, job creation is slowing, while some industries – including manufacturing, automotive, furniture and construction materials – are coming under pressure, according to experts.

Ukrainian refugees boosted the size of Poland’s economy by 2.4% last year, the equivalent of 94 billion zloty (€21.5 billion), according to a new report by the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) and accounting firm Deloitte.

The refugees’ level of employment has now also surpassed that of Polish citizens, but their growing presence in the labour market has had no negative impact on employment or wages for other workers, finds the study.

“Refugees from Ukraine in Poland have entered a new phase characterised by deeper economic integration, increasing labour market participation, and a gradual transition from emergency support mechanisms towards long-term integration into public institutions,” wrote the UNHCR and Deloitte.

The findings come in the latest edition of an annual report analysing the economic impact of Ukrainian refugees, almost one million of whom were living in Poland in 2025.

Modelling carried out by Deloitte showed that their presence is having an increasingly positive effect: in 2025, Ukrainian refugees raised Poland’s GDP by 2.4%, compared to 2.3% in 2024, 2.0% in 2022 and 1.5% in 2022. Deloitte forecasts that the figure will rise to 2.8% by 2035 as Ukrainians integrate further.

The company’s latest figures for 2023 and 2024 differ from those published in last year’s report, with Deloitte saying that it now uses a modelling strategy that is “similar to” but “improved” from before.

The report also notes that the figure for 2025 likely understates the economic impact of Ukrainians who arrived in Poland as refugees, given that many – especially the most economically integrated – have shifted from refugee status to other forms of residency, meaning they do not count towards Deloitte’s data.

 

The employment rate among Ukrainian refugees in Poland rose from 61% in 2023 to 76% in 2025. The latter figure was slightly higher than the rate among Polish citizens.

However, the report notes that Ukrainian refugees are far more likely to be employed on a more precarious basis than native workers: only 42% have standard employment contracts, compared to 80% among Polish citizens.

Ukrainian refugees also much more often work in positions they are overqualified for, while their median wage is only around 85% of the figure among all workers in Poland.

Meanwhile, the report finds that, “contrary to concerns that a large increase in labour supply would negatively affect Polish workers, there is no evidence of deterioration in employment outcomes or wages”. In fact, employment among Polish citizens has continued to rise.

The number of foreign workers in Poland rose 7.2% last year to reach 1.14 million.

Immigrants now make up almost 7% of all workers. While Ukrainians remain by far the largest group, the fastest-growing nationalities last year were Colombians and Indians https://t.co/E0LNJXyyTx

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 9, 2026

Through their high levels of employment, Ukrainian refugees also contribute to Poland’s public finances via taxes and social security contributions. The report estimates that general government revenues are 2.6% higher because of refugee-related economic activity.

Meanwhile, although “the arrival of refugees from Ukraine represented a major stress test for the Polish healthcare system…healthcare expenditures on refugees remain substantially lower on a per-capita basis than expenditures on Polish residents”.

Indeed, in 2025, they paid around 2.8 billion zloty more in health-insurance contributions than the cost of the services they received. At the same time, Poland’s understaffed hospitals have been boosted by the arrival of thousands of Ukrainian doctors, dentists, nurses and midwives.

Ukrainians do have access to Polish social benefits, such as grants for children, but these account for only 10% of income in Ukrainian refugee households. The vast majority, 87%, is earned through work.

Ukrainian immigrants pay more in taxes than they receive in benefits, a report by Poland's National Development Bank has concluded.

The research also indicated that Ukrainians contribute between 0.5% and 2.4% to Poland's annual GDP growth https://t.co/KhXxLtif5W

The report notes that the status of Ukrainian refugees in Poland is becoming increasingly normalised, pointing to changes in Polish government policy introduced earlier this year that meant they no longer had special status.

However, UNHRC’s report also highlights the negative shift in attitudes towards Ukrainian refugees in recent months, with a July poll showing for the first time that a majority of Poles are opposed to accepting refugees from Ukraine.

The ministry then has 90 days to “conduct an administrative investigation into this matter to verify the impact of the transaction on security or public order in Poland”.

 

The ministry can either approve the change of ownership or block the new owner from controlling TVN. In the latter case, the state assets minister, Wojciech Balczun, may order the sale of TVN’s shares.
