The procedure is necessary because the Polish government added TVN and another large private broadcaster, Polsat, to its list of strategic companies in December 2024, bringing them under state protection against takeovers considered aggressive or contrary to the national interest.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Mon, 12 Oct 2026 10:04:25 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.0.7 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Britain’s wealth exodus is only going to get worse https://www.cityam.com/britains-wealth-exodus-is-only-going-to-get-worse/ Mon, 12 Oct 2026 09:55:56 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2464846

Britain must compete to keep its wealthy as countries like Oman offer greater stability, lower taxes and less crime, says Damien Phillips In her speech to close the Conservative conference, Kemi Badenoch’s claim that Britain’s “super wealthy… have all gone” might have been a rhetorical flourish but the exodus of our millionaires is real and [...]]]>

Britain must compete to keep its wealthy as countries like Oman offer greater stability, lower taxes and less crime, says Damien Phillips

In her speech to close the Conservative conference, Kemi Badenoch’s claim that Britain’s “super wealthy… have all gone” might have been a rhetorical flourish but the exodus of our millionaires is real and is only going to get worse 

Britain suffered a tenfold increase in high-net worth individuals fleeing high-tax Britain in just three years, losing around 1,600 millionaires in 2022 and an estimated 16,500 in 2025. Earlier this week, property tycoon David Reuben who shares a family fortune of £28bn, confirmed he had quit the UK for Monaco. In September, we lost hedge-fund billionaire Chris Rokos to Greece. Barely a month seems to go by without another prominent millionaire deciding that Britain is hostile territory for them. 

Recent analysis of the Bloomberg Billionaire’s Index, which didn’t even include Reuben’s departure, showed that ultra-wealthy people worth roughly £121bn have left Britain since Labour came to power in 2024 – this represents more than half of the billionaire wealth associated with the UK.

Competing jurisdications

Many countries like Italy, Switzerland and Monaco are luring them away with a simple proposition – come here and you can preserve your wealth. Switzerland is selling certainty and capital preservation, while Italy allows new residents to avoid being taxed normally and instead pay a €300,000 annual lump sum on foreign income for up to 15 years. 

Others, like the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Singapore and the United States combine favourable treatment of wealth with enormous opportunities to deploy it. For founders and investors, the US offers vast pools of venture capital, highly liquid property markets, tech clusters and enormous consumer demand. Many of those leaving Britain want to create new wealth, not just protect what they have, hence why the US poached 7,500 UK millionaires in 2025 alone. 

Research suggests that global competition for millionaires is also as much about security as it is about tax and opportunities for growth. Wealthy families are looking for places where they and their children feel physically safe and where the political and legal environment is predictable. With nearly nine in ten Brits believing crime and anti-social behaviour are a major national problem and 67 per cent feeling that crime has become worse in the past year, Britain is increasingly unattractive to anyone who doesn’t have to stay here.  

To our chagrin, governments are now actively sharpening their bids to the mobile wealthy and combining all three of these elements into a single deal. Henley’s Wealth Report 2026 singled out Qatar, Bahrain and Oman as “broadening their offerings” as competition for international capital and talent intensifies. 

Oman for instance, whose Sultan is headed to Britain later this month for a state visit, launched a renewable 10-year Golden Residency programme last year aimed at business owners, entrepreneurs and investors that allows them to bring their families and creates a stable, long-term base from which to own, invest in, and run businesses in the country. 

With no income tax and very efficient development, in the World Competitiveness Rankings in 2026 Oman rose to 25th in the world out of 70 economies – just one place behind the UK. On top of this, it ranks third in the world for perceived safety, with 94 per cent of residents saying they feel safe walking alone at night.   

This is the kind of multifaceted package that Britain is now competing against. Yet instead of upping our game, we are talking about yet another tax raising Budget, while Labour-aligned voices call for a wealth tax. The millionaire flight will simply intensify because, as Michael Corleone puts it in The Godfather Part II, Britain’s offer is this: “Nothing”.

Damien Phillips is a fellow of The Cobden Centre and a regular contributor to The Spectator. He has written for CapX, The Critic, ConservativeHome and The Telegraph

The London Stock Exchange is facing “material depopulation” following a boom in the M&A landscape dominated by overseas buyers, a top investment bank has warned. The London Stock Exchange is facing “material depopulation” following a boom in the M&A landscape dominated by overseas buyers, a top investment bank has warned.

Some 42 bids for London-listed firms are currently ongoing with a total market capitalisation of £74bn, according to a new note from Peel Hunt. The figure is more than double the £35bn from the entirety of 2025 across 40 bids.

Overseas bidders make up 64 per cent of the 2026 figures, broadly flat with the previous year.

But the buoyant deals market has come amid a “dearth of IPOs”. Since the start of 2023 there have been 166 bids for firms with a price tag over £100m with the collective value topping £180bn. This is compared to just 11 IPOs above £100 for a total value of £6bn.

“To say that the UK has a problem retaining its companies and listing new ones would be a massive understatement,” said Charles Hall, head of research at Peel Hunt. 

He added the number and value of bids for UK firms were running at “exceptionally high levels, raising concerns that the UK equity market is seeing a material depopulation”.

Airtel Money completed its IPO on the London market last week with a valuation of £5.3bn, marking the biggest listing in five years. It marked the first time since 2021 that the London Stock Exchange landed an IPO north of £1bn.

The City has struggled to compete with the lure of US markets and lost some of its top talent to exchanges across the Atlantic. Money transfer firm Wise downgraded its London listing in favour of New York last year in a major hit to the City bourse.

Since 2023, seven UK giants have shifted their listings, blowing a £120bn hole in the London market. In the same period, seven UK-based firms have also opted to IPO overseas.

“The pace of delistings vs listings in the UK is widening,” one banker told City AM, adding the European markets were “massively lagging the US”.

Calls for government intervention

London AI infrastructure firm Nscale filed for a US listing targeting a $35bn valuation earlier this year, pouring cold water on hopes from stock exchange officials and ministers of attracting high-growth tech talent.

Hall suggested a series of intervention measures to boost equity markets, including shaking up the capital gains regime for domestic and overseas investors and fast-tracking index inclusion. 

“The good news is that turbocharging UK equity markets is not difficult and can be done at pace,” he said.

City minister Lucy Rigby told City AM that capital markets reform was “not a job done” and the government was “continually looking for ways that we can ensure we’re being as competitive as possible”.

Hall pointed to ditching stamp duty on shares as a key lever to “remove friction and enhance UK competitiveness,” adding it makes “no sense for a UK investor to have a higher transaction cost for buying shares in a UK company than a US business”.

In the 2025 Budget, then-Chancellor Rachel Reeves launched a stamp duty holiday, removing the 0.5 per cent levy on UK stocks for newly-listed companies in their first three years of trading.

But the move has failed to open the floodgates for listings. Thought Machine chief Paul Taylor told City AM the levy is “anachronistic” and the recent reforms were not “big enough to really change anybody’s mind either for or against”.

Oil prices remained above the $100 mark on Monday morning after President Trump hailed a deal with Russia’s President Putin that would lead to the supply of millions of barrels of diesel to the US and global markets. 

Brent crude oil futures, a benchmark for international prices, fell by about 0.6 per cent to $104 per barrel. 

This keeps oil prices at high levels as futures were at below $70 per barrel before the Iran war in late February. 

Oil prices heavily influence the global inflation outlook given their significance to critical goods and services. Inflation in the UK is expected to top four per cent in the early parts of next year, according to the Bank of England, while the energy price cap is currently projected to rise by 21 per cent from January. 

Inflation risks highlight the UK economy’s vulnerability to President Trump’s decisions and global conflicts.

On Friday, Donald Trump said he had a 90-minute call with Vladimir Putin, in which Russia agreed to supply more than 2.25m barrels of diesel to the US, which is equivalent to less than a day of supply in the US. Russia agreed to supply another 500,000 tonnes of diesel, approximately 3.75m barrels, next month. 

The US president later claimed that Ukraine’s President Zelensky and President Putin had agreed to a ceasefire for attacks on energy infrastructure, with Trump attributing a rise in diesel prices in America to Ukraine’s strikes in Russia. 

Zelensky said the ceasefire was “news” to him and later said that Russia had hit a power plant in Kyiv after Trump’s impromptu announcement. He also told ABC News that the rise in international energy prices was “because of the war in the Middle East, of the blocking of Hormuz”.  

 Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he welcomed the call for a ceasefire and added attacks were coming from Russia. 

Oil price spike to lead to spending erosion

Trump also piled pressure on Zelensky by saying the Ukrainian leader should step aside. Zelensky said he would announce elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day total ceasefire. 

Separately, strikes by the Houthis, an Iran-backed militia, at Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia has further intensified hostilities in the Middle East, which shows fewer signs of drawing to a close. 

The fractures in Western relationships come at a difficult time for Burnham and Chancellor John Healey as the Office for Budget Responsibility adjusts its economic forecasts ahead of the Budget. 

The Institute for Fiscal Studies said on Monday that the Chancellor would likely need to find £35bn extra in spending by 2031 in order to prevent real term cuts to department budgets as higher inflation is set to erode the value of expenditure.

HMV is set to close its flagship Oxford Street store just three years after its comeback to the location where it was founded more than a century ago.  The music and entertainment retailer said the site will shut its doors in March next year, blaming a doubled rent bill and the cost of “substantial” renovations.  [...]]]>

HMV is set to close its flagship Oxford Street store just three years after its comeback to the location where it was founded more than a century ago. 

The music and entertainment retailer said the site will shut its doors in March next year, blaming a doubled rent bill and the cost of “substantial” renovations. 

The departure of the historic outlet from Europe’s busiest shopping destination comes as retailers urge the government to help high street businesses weather soaring rents and taxes. 

HMV opened its inaugural store on Oxford Street in 1921 but was forced to close the site in 2019 after the chain tumbled into administration. 

The business was rescued by Canadian retail tycoon Doug Putman’s Sunrise Records when he bought 100 HMV shops, saving 1,500 jobs. 27 stores collapsed, costing 455 jobs. 

HMV, which now operates at 123 locations across the UK, returned to Oxford Street in 2023 after securing a fresh deal with landlords. Putman had hailed the chain’s return as a “great moment” in its recovery.

But Phil Halliday, HMV’s managing director, announced on Monday that the company will be retreating from Oxford Street once again. 

‘Frustrating’ setback for HMV

He said: “This is a special store, it’s where we began 100 years ago and bringing it back to life in 2023 was a big moment in our recent history.

“It’s frustrating that it has been made commercially unviable. However, we are looking ahead, and our focus is now on what we do to make exciting steps for HMV in 2027.”

The retailer said its recovery is gaining momentum despite this setback, pointing to the 15 per cent like-for-like sales growth it has achieved so far this year. 

HMV is on track to notch £240m in revenue across its in-store and online estate this year, which would mark a 13 per cent improvement on last year’s £212m.

Halliday added: “We hope to redeploy affected team members through other London stores and head office roles and are exploring ways to minimise the impact on jobs while we seek a new flagship site.

“We’re actively looking for a new location in the West End and are determined to give London a store that music fans can be proud of.”

]]> 2464831Felix Armstrong Felix Armstrong Zack Polanski’s Greens are a toxic mix of hatred and economic illiteracy https://www.cityam.com/zack-polanskis-greens-are-a-toxic-mix-of-hatred-and-economic-illiteracy/ Mon, 12 Oct 2026 09:13:17 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2464818

The Green party’s antisemitic ‘Zionism is racism’ motion puts them bizarrely at odds with the Palestinian Liberation Organization, which recognises the state of Israel. And on the economy, their policies are simply delusional, says Eliot Wilson At its recent conference in Brighton, the Green Party of England and Wales affirmed a set of policies which, [...]]]>

The Green party’s antisemitic ‘Zionism is racism’ motion puts them bizarrely at odds with the Palestinian Liberation Organization, which recognises the state of Israel. And on the economy, their policies are simply delusional, says Eliot Wilson

At its recent conference in Brighton, the Green Party of England and Wales affirmed a set of policies which, in Yes, Minister terms would, be described as “bold”, even “courageous”. It is now the task of party leader Zack Polanski, fresh from his narrow defeat in last week’s Holborn and St Pancras by-election, to forge a coherent, popular and credible policy platform.

Different parties approach their annual conferences differently. The Labour Party conference allows delegates of affiliated organisations (principally trades unions) and of constituency associations to vote on policies but these votes are non-binding.

The Conservatives, by contrast, have never included the annual gathering of members in the decision-making process, regarding it instead as a networking, entertaining and, often, plotting opportunity. AJ Balfour, the patrician, philosophically sceptical Prime Minister from 1902 to 1905, famously said, “I would as soon be guided by the views of my valet as by the Conservative Party Conference”. Good valets are hard to find.

The Green Party allows members to submit and vote on binding policy motions directly. At its recent conference one motion stated that Zionism is racism “based upon European settler-colonial systems of domination and oppression”, declared the Greens an anti-Zionist party and called for “a single democratic Palestinian State between the Jordan river and the Mediterranean Sea with equal rights for all”.

This puts them at odds with the traditional mantra of a “two-state solution” and at odds, bizarrely, with Fatah, the dominant faction of the Palestine Liberation Organization, which recognises the State of Israel. It is yet further at odds with reality, if Greens think a single state of Palestine “from the river to the sea” would be safe for the region’s 7.5m Jews. But reality and the safety of Jewish populations do not feature high up on the party’s list of priorities.

Statist philosophy

On the economy, trumpeting its desire to “put people and planet ahead of fiscal rules” – perhaps not British history’s most catchy political slogan – the conference affirmed a number of significant policies. They fall under the dim-bulb assertion that we must go “beyond an obsession with GDP and interest rates to focus on what really matters: improving people’s lives”. GDP is a metric, a way of measuring how prosperous a country is. The idea that interest rates have no bearing on “improving people’s lives” is also a peculiar one.

The overall philosophy is profoundly statist. The Greens advocate “greater public control of banking and finance and more public investment to prioritise essential services”, which is another way of saying they want to spend more taxpayers’ money on public services, and “into affordable homes, good jobs and the green transition”. A publicly owned retail bank, “a network of local and regional community banks to fund small and medium businesses” and limits on the size of private banks indicate a party fundamentally opposed to private wealth.

The conference called for more to be spent on “the real National Health Service we deserve”, with all forms of care delivered exclusively by the state and including dentistry, optometry and pharmaceutical products. This amounts to ever-greater spending on healthcare as the population ages and treatments become more widespread, more elaborate and more expensive. This is missing the point on a grand scale: it is hard to look at the NHS over the past 20 years and conclude that the problem has been too little spending on too few services.

Inevitably there has been support for a three-year emergency brake on rental costs. Rents will not rise “above CPI, wage growth or two per cent  – whichever is lowest”, following which there would be a national Fair Rent Guarantee. In practical terms, this is rigging the housing market. We know that rent controls in New York, San Francisco and Berlin, at least, discouraged investment and adequate maintenance as well as causing shortages of appropriate provision, while entrenching existing tenants.

Given a shortage of housing in the UK, the effects of discouraging more landlords from entering the market and reducing the margins of renting could be catastrophic. But the long-term real-world effects fade away for the Greens with the dopamine hit of performative virtue in public policy.

To this shopping list must be added a new system of social care, which “should be available to everyone who needs it and free at the point of use, just like the NHS is for healthcare”. The Greens themselves estimate this £20bn.

Where does the money come from for all of this? The Greens want a wealth tax of one per cent on individual assets above £10m and two per cent on assets above £1bn, as well as aligning Capital Gains Tax rates with income tax and applying National Insurance to investment income.

For the Greens, taxation and expenditure are only distantly linked (and only because voters prefer at least a loose association between how much of their money the government is taking and what they are getting in return)

Wealth taxes are extraordinarily difficult to implement: Austria, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Finland, Luxembourg and Sweden all introduced wealth taxes in the 1990s and 2000s, and by 2007 all had repealed them. But remember what Zack Polanski told the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg about a wealth tax last autumn: “This isn’t about creating public investment, we can do that anyway, we don’t need to tax the wealthy to do that… it’s ultimately about reducing inequality.”

For the Greens, taxation and expenditure are only distantly linked (and only because voters prefer at least a loose association between how much of their money the government is taking and what they are getting in return). Their maxim in l’état, c’est nous: the state is the primary and preferred device for creating a society in their image, and that means much greater use of legislative and fiscal coercion combined with unsustainable financial binges on favoured projects.

Current polling puts the Greens on around 10 per cent, scrapping with the Liberal Democrats for fourth place, and facing the prospect of being reduced to just two MPs. But politics is volatile, and if Polanski embraces the malign prescription of his party’s conference, he has a seductive but always disastrous offer for the electorate: we can give you everything you want, and someone else will pay.

We are all that “someone else” and we would all pay. But history shows us the potency of die große Lüge, the “big lie”. A vast, sweeping untruth is much more likely to be believed. Let’s hope voters do not believe those spun by the Greens in Brighton earlier this month.

Eliot Wilson is a writer and historian

The under-fire chairwoman of King Charles’s favourite interior design firm has hit back at the “distracting” investor plot to remove her. 

Dame Dianne Thompson, chair of London-listed Sanderson Design Group, wrote to shareholders on Monday urging them to slap down a major investor’s “disruptive” attempts to oust her. 

LBV Asset Management, which owns 12 per cent of Sanderson, has been pushing for the removal of Dame Thompson, a former National Lottery boss, over the designer’s drift towards “inaction and inertia”. 

The historic wallpaper maker holds a Royal Warrant and earlier this year hosted King Charles at its new headquarters, but the investor claims new leadership is needed to kick off a “sustained period of change”. 

Shareholders supportive of LBV’s coup attempt have hit out at the “lavish” redesign of Sanderson’s new headquarters, its slow expansion in the US and the “unjustified” decision to hand the chief executive and finance boss 36 per cent of the group’s profit in pay deals.

But Sanderson has vowed to fight off this investor pressure, urging shareholders to vote against LBV’s motions at the emergency meeting it has called for 29 October. 

Dame Thompson told shareholders on Monday: “When considering the strength of the Group’s performance, together with LBV’s stated support for the executive management team and operational strategy, I believe it right to question whether LBV’s underlying intention is aligned to that of the wider shareholder base.

“LBV’s proposals risk significant disruption and uncertainty at precisely the point when the benefits of the Group’s transformation are becoming increasingly evident.”

Investor pressure ‘unnecessary and distracting’

The design firm’s chair pointed to the company’s latest figures as proof of “continued momentum”. Revenue jumped six per cent to £51m and pre-tax profit grew by two thirds to £2.5m in the six months to the end of July.

Dame Thompson, aged 75, told investors that Sanderson had set out plans for her eventual retirement before LBV sought to force her early exit. 

The group’s board had already decided that it would begin searching for Dame Thompson’s successor in January 2027, she said. “Good governance requires proper succession planning, not the immediate removal of a Chair and the abandonment of an established process at a point when the Company’s strategy is beginning to deliver.”

Sanderson’s board also wrote to investors on Monday, setting out its support of Dame Thompson. It said: “Dame Dianne’s leadership experience across major consumer businesses remains highly relevant to the Group, and the Board has full confidence in her continued contribution throughout this process.”

The board also set out to prove that it is engaging “constructively” with LBV, handing shareholders proof of 20 times it has met with the representatives of the investor since September 2024. 

Sanderson’s board pointed to its association with King Charles as proof that the design group is still relevant. The firm unveiled its Highgrove collection last year, inspired by the gardens of the King’s Gloucestershire estate.

The collection, which gained “personal approval” from the King, “has been the most successful launch to date and created a clear halo effect on the broader Sanderson brand,” the board said.

Sanderson told shareholders it will fight off all pressure from LBV. “The Board considers the resulting uncertainty to be unnecessary and distracting, and a risk to the Group’s positive momentum and focused strategy.”

Shares in Sanderson Design Group gained 2.6 per cent to 79p in early trading.

    Within the unregulated waters of whisky cask investment schemes, there be sharks. The sector has certainly had a bad press, and there has been lots of squabbling and finger-pointing, often by those with a vested interest. Tom Bruce-Gardyne lifts the lid on this murky world for City AM’s Whisky Business.

    “Let me take you into the ruthless world of the multi-million-pound whisky scams,” declares intrepid reporter Samantha Poling.

    “The sharks are circling. They know there’s blood. They can smell it,” adds whisky cask broker and independent bottler, Kenny Macdonald. “Unfortunately, in this particular case, the blood is whisky.”

    It was a stirring start to her BBC exposé – ‘Hunting the Whisky Bandits’, first broadcast in March last year. The victims are real enough, having lost their life savings in casks of whisky that were eye-wateringly overpriced or never even existed. But the evil perpetrators are almost cartoon-like. 

    In a sting operation, we meet convicted fraudster Craig, think sharp-suited Apprentice contestant, only ten times worse, and his blonde sidekick, who apparently doubles as an eyebrow technician from Essex. Seeing them in the flesh, you wouldn’t buy a used paperclip, let alone a second-hand car, from either of them. 

    The outing of such pantomime villains has provoked a great deal of finger-pointing from other cask investment firms, and cries of ‘trust me, not them’, says Isabel Graham-Yooll of the independent rare spirits consultancy, Wisgy.

    She sees it as a distraction from the core issue. “The real problem is people being sold things as an investment that has nowhere near the value they’re being charged,” she says.

    As Kenny Macdonald points out, the 2019 Knight Frank Wealth Report sparked the gold rush in cask investments by quoting a very particular index compiled by Rare Whisky 101 of what were claimed to be the 100 ‘most desirable’ bottles of rare whisky. 

    Had you bought them 10 years earlier, you could have made a 580 per cent return. Then again, had you picked the winners in the last ten Grand Nationals, you would have made even more.     Far from a cycling decline, unused bike parking at offices proves London’s developers have solved the wrong problem, writes Lime’s head of government relations Stef Lehmann 

    An empty office bike rack tells you where someone hasn’t stored their own bike for eight (if you’re lucky) hours. It doesn’t tell you anything about how people are getting to work.

    That distinction has been missing from the debate about unused cycle storage in London’s office buildings. Research from the London Property Alliance found that around three quarters of cycle parking spaces in the 21 office buildings it studied were vacant at peak times. Developers have a fair point: space should earn its keep. But it is a leap from there to concluding that London needs less cycle parking.

    Seen in isolation, the research could make it sound like cycling is ailing in one of Europe’s largest metropolitan areas. In reality, the opposite is true: London has seen record cycling levels over the last few years.

    Transport for London (TfL) estimates that daily cycle trips rose by 12 per cent in 2025, to 1.4m. That’s the highest it’s ever been, and recent TfL data also shows that at least one in 10 cycling trips – we suspect more – are made on shared e-bikes. 

    What has changed is the choice of bike. You can now cycle to the office without owning one, leaving it behind that evening because of one too many drinks, worrying about it being stolen in the meantime, or finding the space to store it at home. (This Is Awkward has some great examples of the latter.) Some are so attached to this way of getting home now that they resort to rather inadvisable behaviours. No repeat of the Tube strike Lime Hunger Games, please.

    Obviously, no one is suggesting that all secure underground bike racks are suddenly turned into shared e-bike parking. But we are suggesting two other things.

    We want to work with private landowners

    Firstly, if developers are concerned about that space going to waste just to satisfy a now dated city planning requirement, making alternative outside space available for shared e-bike parking should also count.

    Secondly, we want to hear from private landowners who have space for shared e-bike parking more widely – because there isn’t enough of it in London.

    No shared e-bike operator goes a day without hearing about overcrowded parking bays. Some of this is in the nature of the service we provide: no one can predict where every journey goes, because we don’t run on rails or along set routes. Lime’s on-street team of more than 400 people therefore moves around our vehicles throughout the day, every day, based on those travel patterns that are regular and predictable. 

    The more fundamental issue, though, is that shared e-bike parking has struggled to keep pace with demand. Operators must contribute to tackling this, and Lime has committed £5m to a London Parking Fund as part of our £20m London Action Plan – £1.5m of which is already being spent by boroughs as part of the first tranche. But funding is not always the biggest challenge. Everyone knows how contested London’s street space is, and some changes to how space is allocated can create winners and losers – costing precious political capital.

    This is where private land comes in. We can work directly with the landowner so that installing a funded parking bay takes far less time. And there’s a knock-on benefit: increasing bay supply across London, particularly in the most high-demand areas in the City and Westminster, will take progressively more pressure off overstretched individual bays.

    Private land won’t solve every parking problem. But it can help deliver more space where people need it, without waiting for every solution to come from the public highway and local councils.

    So our view is that operators, boroughs and developers should be looking at the best use of London’s public realm together. If some private cycle storage is underused while nearby shared bays are full, regulations should take changing travel habits into account and pivot to shared e-bike parking. Developers can still have their basement gyms too – and officegoers can extend their post-exercise high by cycling home.

    Stef Lehmann is head of government relations at Lime UK & Ireland

    Protecting heritage does not always mean preventing change, writes Chris Hayward ahead of the publication of the City Plan 2040

    Over the past few weeks I’ve had the opportunity to speak to politicians and business figures at all five major party conferences.

    Whatever the political differences between them, there is now broad recognition that Britain needs to invest, build and compete more effectively if it is to raise productivity and living standards.

    Closer to home, the planning inspectorate is about to publish its final report, and sign off, on our local development plan (City Plan 2040), bringing one of the most closely watched planning processes in the country towards its conclusion.

    For the City of London, and indeed the rest of the UK, it’s significant because it will provide the framework that guides development in the nation’s most productive Square Mile for years to come.

    Developers needs long-term certainty

    Britain cannot increase productivity, attract investment or remain internationally competitive if major development is routinely held in limbo. Those businesses making long-term decisions need certainty, the investors committing billions of pounds need confidence, and the planning system has a vital role to play in delivering both.

    The City’s plan has been many years in the making, undergoing multiple rounds of consultation, extensive scrutiny and public examination. Yet despite that process, uncertainty persisted and during that period, developers, investors and occupiers were left waiting for clarity.

    Unfortunately, that experience is not unique to the City. Across the country, we hear the same concerns from businesses looking to invest. They can handle tough standards and requirements, but what they struggle with is unpredictability. When similar proposals can receive different responses depending on where or when they are considered, confidence suffers. Businesses can adapt to clear expectations, but they are far less able to account for a system where outcomes are uncertain and decisions do not always align with the published policy framework.

    The best planning systems are economic accelerators. They give businesses the confidence to invest, developers the certainty to build and communities a clear vision of how places will evolve. When decisions are timely, consistent and rooted in a stable plan, capital flows more freely, homes and workplaces are delivered faster, and talented people can live and work where they are most productive. The result is higher growth, greater prosperity and stronger, better-connected cities.

    But when decisions are slow, inconsistent or unpredictable, uncertainty increases, projects are delayed, costs rise and investment can go elsewhere. In that situation, the planning system stops being an enabler of growth and becomes an obstacle to it.

    Balancing growth with heritage

    Of course, planning is about more than economic development alone. One of the central questions considered during the City Plan process has been how to balance growth with the protection of heritage, and I believe passionately that London’s success has always been built on combining the two.

    Around the Tower of London, that balance has been examined in exceptional detail and the independent Planning Inspectorate has found that we get that balance right.

    The Tower of London sits beside a City that has evolved continuously for centuries. Heritage is one of our greatest strengths. It attracts visitors, investment and global recognition. But it does not follow that protecting heritage means preventing change.

    The challenge for planners is to find a sensible balance and City Plan does exactly that. It supports the delivery of new, much needed commercial space where it can be accommodated, while maintaining strong protections for heritage assets, strategic views and the character of the capital.

    At a time when some predicted the decline of city centres, London has remained one of the world’s leading destinations for business, finance and innovation. Companies still want to be in places with talent, connectivity and opportunity. The question is whether we will provide the space needed to support that demand.

    In the Square Mile, we cannot grow outwards, so we have to grow intelligently, concentrating development where it is most appropriate, retrofitting and creating better public spaces, to ensure growth ambitions are working alongside the historic environment rather than the two against each other.

    As the government rightly focuses on growth, there is an opportunity to learn a wider lesson from the City Plan process, which is that successful planning systems are not those that always say yes, but systems that project authority and confidence.

    Confidence that decisions will be taken in a timely way. Confidence in planning policies and their clarity, so that developers and investors understand the rules. And confidence that growth and stewardship can sit alongside one another.

    For the City of London, the publication of the Planning Inspectorate’s report will give us one of the most powerful tools we have to support economic growth, strengthen confidence and shape the future success of our cities.

    The challenge now is to ensure the system can be consistent, nationally, to help deliver that ambition.

    Chris Hayward is the policy chairman for the City of London Corporation

    Sport fans aren’t just consumers but stakeholders so what Manchester City say during their crisis could be existential for them, write Jess Chan and Matthew Gilleard.

    “Some people believe football is a matter of life and death…I can assure you it is much, much more important than that.”

    So said Bill Shankly, encapsulating both sport’s penchant for hyperbole and the undeniable strength of attachment that people feel to football.

    The sentiment shows why, when it comes to sports, crisis communications is a different ball game – one where fans and rivals alike will storm the field and impact the outcome. 

    Since the publication of findings that Manchester City had breached Premier League regulations, the pitch invasion has been swift and overwhelming. 

    With far-reaching implications and hordes of rival fans smelling blood, the communications field has been flooded with commentary.

    The tribal nature of English football means that fans are active brand champions. They are both investors in, and influencers of, the reputation of the organisation they follow. So when crisis hits, supporters are not spectators but stakeholders. 

    Wimbledon and European Super League offer lessons

    Management of this key stakeholder group is critical. As Oliver Reed’s Proximo tells gladiator Maximus: “Win the crowd and you will win your freedom”. 

    Fan fervour among rival clubs is unlikely to be swayed by anything that City say, but if the club lose their own fanbase, disaster turns into genuine existential threat. 

    This is a unique characteristic of the sports world. Apple or Tesla may have cult-like followings, with customers blindly devoted to their products and vision, but football fandom is something else entirely. 

    You don’t buy an iPhone because you have core memories of your parents taking you to your first Apple Store as a child. Your grandparents did not stand on the Tesla terraces in years gone by. 

    Football clubs are central to this nation’s heritage and cultural identity. Fans are not merely followers or consumers of a product, but the very fabric of a club. Players, managers, even owners come and go, but the fan collective is a constant.

    Wimbledon FC’s relocation to Milton Keynes and the backlash to the European Super League show us that overlooking a fanbase can be a fatal error reputationally. 

    So when times get tough, an organisation’s communications approach must be mindful of this dynamic. 

    Tactical analysis: Time to settle for a draw?

    The club has thus far been strident and bullish in its communications. In an arena like sport, where teams are expected to fight for every hard-earned victory on the pitch, fans may be pleased to see City staunchly defending the club off the pitch.

    But they, too, will ultimately want answers and certainty.

    In the other dugout, rival clubs’ supporters and other commentators will continue to challenge the club’s position.

    Former Manchester United captain Roy Keane has said he would throw his winners’ medals in the bin if implicated in such a verdict, while other pundits have called for titles and owners to be removed. 

    Opposing fan vitriol will not die down, nor be swayed by City’s statements. But the club must carefully consider their communications, and stubborn ownership must not risk City’s own fans turning against them. 

    In face-saving terms, the playbook now is surely the equivalent of settling for a draw rather than walking away with nothing. 

    The reputation game: City must earn trust

    Reputations are built on trust and success – both of which lie at the heart of the Manchester City issue. 

    The successes are already being called into question. Trust cannot be completely lost too, otherwise the reputational rebuild will be that much harder.

    The club’s communications around how they defend and explain their actions and how they respond to the fate that awaits will define fan trust and belief in the organisation going forward. Against this backdrop, Shankly’s words might not seem so hyperbolic after all.

    Jess Chan is a reputation consultant and Matthew Gilleard is a communications consultant at Infinite.

    If there has been a dominant trend this year with new restaurant openings, it’s the unending rise of the Greek taverna. It feels apt. The same year that pavements cracked with heat and parks turned brittle, a yearning for the Hellenic feels natural. And the Odyssey came out, which felt weirdly foreign in its dark dampness this July.

    The taverna is a semi chaotic, elbow-pressed testament to grilled meats and oregano-spiked salads. In Athens this summer, I ate bowls of brothy chickpeas at Diporto and in the evening, beef livers and lamb pilaf at Manari Tavern. Back in London, Greek food is hardly groundbreaking, but a new generation of restaurants is very much in vogue. It’s dippier with more bread varietals. The plates and chops are a little smaller, the rooms more contrived in a gesture towards tradition or an attempt at rupture from it. In effect, London-accented. From tasting menus to family favourites, it’s all Greekish in the city.

    Oma & Agora

    Oma (Michelin-starred upstairs) and Agora (not Michelin-starred downstairs) are two restaurants in the same building in Borough. Set up by David Carter – who recently set up the much-hyped and much-punned Kid – the restaurants are the originators of the new Greek wave. Oma is ‘inspired by the isles of greece’, Agora is ‘inspired by the streets and markets of athens’. Here the emphasis is on flatbreads, dips, sweetly charred skewers and fire cooking. 

    Maza

    Maza is Mayfair Greek: buzzy and pricey. Tables are pressed together as the well-heeled touch heels. This place has captured the plate-clattering energy of a good taverna, and the taramasalata is pretty perfect too. Owner Christina Mouratoglou says that she wanted to create “fun, warm, organised chaos” when she opened the restaurant earlier this spring as Greek food mainlined into the “mainstream”. Maza ticks those boxes. On the other side of London is Lagana, which opened last year and feels a bit like the Shoreditch crayon-drawn doppelgänger of Maza. Both guarantee a good night out. 

    Zylia

    Zylia was London’s most hyped opening this year until the next one. It also stirred up a touch of controversy over whether it properly marketed itself as Greek or Cypriot, or a mix of all the food in a palatable jumble of convenience. It’s headed by Nick Molyviatis (family from Athens), an ex-Kiln head chef, and Barry Karacostas (family from Cyprus). As expected from a Kiln alum, the flavour is packing. The milk-fed lamb shoulder is a particular highlight.

    Pyro

    Another Borough spot, upmarket beach-shack-coded Pyro nods towards the fine-dining end of the spectrum with a tasting menu. Chef Yiannis Mexis, who has worked at Hide and The Ledbury, has created a contemporary, cheffy take on his native cuisine. Some highlights include spanakopita transformed into a Parmesan-dusted nata tart and iberico pork souvlaki. They also serve a room-dividing tzatziki cocktail that tastes just like tzatziki. 

    Andy’s Greek Taverna

    On the other end of the spectrum is Andy’s with its big ol’ slabs of moussaka and stuffed peppers. A Camden institution serving souvlaki and gyros since the 60s, Andy’s is not the best Greek restaurant in London, but it’s comforting and has one of my favourite restaurant websites of all time (volume up).

    Bagatelle has opened inside Chelsea’s Stamford Bridge. Matt Hardy went down to see if it lives up to its reputation.

    It feels like every week a top football club opens a new hospitality offering that claims to reinvent what has, in reality, long been the status quo: a good bit of food and a free bar.

    That changed, pretty dramatically, when Fulham opened their Riverside Stand with its £20,000 season tickets, Michelin-starred chefs and tidal wave of cocktails.

    City AM was told that this offering – seen as one of the best across the Premier League’s 20 clubs – had been topped in another corner of south west London. So, naturally, we had to investigate.

    If you were to search for Bagatelle on TikTok just a few months ago you’d have been met with youngsters – 20 to 40 somethings – in Saint-Tropez trying their very best to enjoy themselves in the sweaty French summer.

    Do the same search today and you’ll find a very similar clientele – only inside Chelsea’s Stamford Bridge instead.

    Bagatelle describes itself as a “French hospitality brand of luxury restaurants and beach clubs”. So why has it gone into football, and why Chelsea?

    Bagatelle… at Chelsea?

    “Chelsea are world champions, they’re known around the world, they sit in probably the most affluent postcode in sports,” Bagatelle International co-founder Salima Vellani tells City AM.

    “Moving into sports was kind of the new flex for us in terms of where the brand is going – it’s more of a luxury lifestyle platform, not just a restaurant group.

    “We know where our clients want us to be and so we’re moving in that direction. And sports is missing this layer and it’s never been done in Premier League football.”

    The 80-cover offering is, frankly, a little odd. As a sports fan you wouldn’t have known you were at one of the capital’s great sporting arenas. As a Chelsea fan – which the lady next to me was – it may borderline on infuriating.

    Getting a ticket at Chelsea is difficult as it is, especially with a number of seats being converted from general admission to hospitality. But Vellani rightly points out that they have instead taken seats away from other premium areas of the ground, rather than general admission.

    “I have a brand that I have to protect,” she says. “What I don’t want to do is go in and fit into your box. What I need is [that] you fit into our vision.

    “[Chelsea] and Legends, which operates the stadium, are phenomenal partners, they agreed to do it and said, ‘Let’s create something totally different that’s never been seen before’.

    “I wanted to create a new category. We’ve been pioneers in the restaurant space, let’s be pioneers in the sports space. I saw a gap, and that gap is luxury VIP hospitality as opposed to what they call premium.”

    The reality

    What Bagatelle at Stamford Bridge is, however, is perfectly designed for a specific group of people; those who want to experience football their own way. 

    Vellani says the offering has been popular with women; at last month’s Hull City game the clientele was predominantly female. 

    She says it allows players, their partners and high-level guests to relax. John Terry, harassed for a picture only once or twice, certainly looked at ease.

    It has a place in football, and those who hate that may not quite understand how the game has evolved. The food – ranging from tuna tartare to steak to full-time pizzas – was exceptional. The booze – often prescriptive in these settings – was plentiful and wide-ranging.

With ticket prices in line with other major sporting events and well below some such as the recent football World Cup – albeit staged in the more commercialised North American market – cricket should be proud that we have a summer-long event that draws the crowds, no matter what. What’s better than a 10-hour sporting hospitality day, after all?

    Corporate hospitality at sport may have been unforgettable in the past because of the amount of booze on offer. Those boisterous “boys’ days out” are now long gone, however; at today’s events the wine list gets genuine attention, as do the selection of non-alcoholic beers and mocktails.

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Why a recycled password is worth money

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

Each of those requirements targets the behaviour the extension recorded: a handful of memorable strings, nudged sideways by a digit, stretched across an entire online life.

The standard now assumes a machine is doing the remembering. Anyone who ever stuck a “1” on the end to get past a signup form was just covering the shift until it arrived.

A Dutch court sided with a worker who refused constant video surveillance, forcing his employer to pay damages—a warning shot across the evolving battle over remote work monitoring.]]>

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

How common all-day camera rules are

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Where the line actually falls

Whatever this settles, it settles in one jurisdiction, on one set of facts, at the lowest rung of the court system. Article 8 offers nothing in Florida, where employment is generally at will and can end without a stated reason, subject to the usual exceptions for discrimination, retaliation and whatever a contract says.

What the case supplies is a price tag on a boundary that remote-work policy has been drifting across without much thought: supervising the work is one thing, keeping a lens open in somebody’s house for the length of a shift is another. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

Markus Villig was 19 in 2013, fresh out of high school in Tallinn, and frustrated with how hard it was to get a reliable taxi in his own city. He borrowed €5,000 from his family to build a first version of an app, then did the unglamorous part himself: walking up to taxi drivers on the street in Tallinn and persuading them, one at a time, to sign up. Villig’s own €5,000 loan covered exactly one prototype. Everything after that came from investors willing to bet that Bolt’s low-cost, fast-mover approach would eventually outlast better-funded rivals in the markets it entered. Operating profit told a similar story of a company just crossing the line, at €19.5 million, reversed from the prior year’s €87.7 million loss. A margin that thin is not really a statement about profitability so much as a statement about intent. Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. Out of it has come ten companies that reached a billion-dollar valuation at some point in their history, among them Skype, Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive, Playtech and Veriff, according to Invest in Estonia’s own tally.

Using CB Insights’ underlying company data alongside that population figure, a figure Invest in Estonia and outlets including Fintech Baltic put at roughly 7.1 unicorns per million residents, based on Invest in Estonia’s cumulative count of companies that have ever reached $1B — not a live ranking CB Insights itself publishes, second only to Liechtenstein and more than three times the United States’ rate of about 2.2 per million.

The tiger leap that came before the unicorns

This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. Its goal was blunt: wire the country’s schools for computers and the internet as a deliberate act of catching up. It worked faster than almost anyone expected.

The rollout was rapid but not instantaneous. Education Estonia says all schools had computers by 2000 and all were connected to the internet by 2001. Two decades later, in 2014, the government extended the same instinct outward with e-Residency, a digital identity scheme that lets people anywhere in the world register and run an Estonian company online, without granting them any right to actually live there. Neither programme produced a unicorn by itself. What they produced was a population that treated computers as ordinary tools a generation before most of Europe did, and a legal and administrative system built to let a small number of people start companies with very little friction.

The first of the ten billion-dollar companies was Skype, built in Tallinn in 2003. Skype itself has since been folded into Microsoft and no longer exists as a standalone business, but it left something behind in Tallinn that the other nine companies on the list arguably needed first: a generation of engineers and early employees who had already helped build something that scaled to hundreds of millions of users, and who knew, from direct experience, that it could be done from Estonia rather than London or Silicon Valley.

According to the company’s own account of its founding, on Wise’s own history page, the two of them started by simply swapping money directly with each other every month, at the real mid-market exchange rate, to avoid their banks’ fees and markups. They launched TransferWise, later renamed Wise, in 2011, and it went public in London a decade later, making both founders Estonia’s first tech billionaires.

It wasn’t only talent that recirculated. Toivo Annus, one of Skype’s founding engineers who led its engineering team until the eBay sale, went on to co-found Ambient Sound Investments with three other early Skype engineers in 2003, a private investment firm that has since backed more than 50 early-stage ventures, according to documented accounts of his career. Annus died in 2020, but the firm he helped start is still one of the more active early-stage investors operating out of Tallinn, another channel through which Skype’s original payout kept funding whatever came next.

The ecosystem underneath those ten companies is larger and more active than the unicorn count alone suggests. Estonian startups collectively reported €3.9 billion in revenue in 2024, up 14.7 percent on the year before, according to Invest in Estonia’s own sector figures, and the sector now employs about 14,400 people directly, or roughly one in every 38 working Estonians, at an average monthly salary of €3,650, more than double the national average. A per-capita unicorn count says nothing about how many of those companies are still worth a billion dollars today, still headquartered in Estonia, or profitable. Playtech moved its primary listing to London years ago. Skype no longer trades as an independent business at all. What the figure does capture, reliably, is how much outsized technology output a small population has produced relative to its size, whatever has happened to any individual company since, and how much of that output traces back to a single, now-defunct voice-calling app and the state’s own earlier bet on wiring its classrooms. For a country with fewer people than a mid-sized American county, that is the more durable claim.
