Amazon Web Services (AWS) today launched an open-source Physical AI Toolchain designed to help roboticists move from collecting data to training, simulating, validating and deploying AI models on their robots.

The toolchain brings together AWS services and NVIDIA’s Physical AI software stack into a single development workflow. The goal is to address one of the biggest challenges facing companies developing AI-powered robots: connecting the many pieces required to turn a trained model into a system that can reliably operate in the real world.

“We’re trying to make this easy button, if you will, so that people can actually focus on the problem that they’re trying to solve rather than having to worry about all of the infrastructure,” Sri Elaprolu, director of Frontier AI Science and Engineering at AWS, told The Robot Report.

The Physical AI Toolchain is not a direct replacement for RoboMaker, a  cloud-based robotics simulation platform that was shut down in 2025. Elaprolu described RoboMaker as one of the components of AWS’s robotics stack, while the new toolchain brings together a broader set of development technologies.

From data to deployment

The toolchain combines five pieces of the AI development process: synthetic data generation, model training, simulation and validation, edge deployment, and continuous improvement. A robotics company could collect demonstrations of a robot performing a task, generate additional training scenarios synthetically, train or fine-tune a model, and test that model in simulation before deploying it to a physical robot.

AWS uses Amazon SageMaker for model training and AWS IoT Greengrass for distributing models to edge devices. NVIDIA’s contributions include Isaac Sim, Isaac Lab, Isaac GR00T and Cosmos. Companies can use the components individually or combine them into an end-to-end workflow.

“The amount of data that you need to train these models is significant, and there’s not a lot of data that’s available, unlike LLMs where there’s a ton of data on the internet,” Elaprolu said. “So how do you generate that data? How do you generate synthetic data that is representative of the real world? That’s one of the things that we’re trying to solve.”

Synthetic data can help companies generate additional scenarios, while simulation lets developers test models before deploying them to physical hardware. The toolchain supports a feedback loop in which data collected by robots in the field is returned to the cloud and used to improve models.

“As you start scaling out these robotic deployments, the learnings that get captured locally need to be flown back into the cloud,” Elaprolu said. “So you continually iterate the brain.”

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

Lessons from Amazon’s robots

Elaprolu said the toolchain includes lessons from Amazon’s own robotics operations, which now include more than 1 million robots. But Amazon’s controlled fulfillment centers don’t represent every environment where Physical AI will operate.

Elaprolu pointed to Japanese robotics company Telexistence, which is deploying humanoids in convenience stores. More than 300 have been deployed, he said, with more expected. Unlike a controlled factory, a convenience store introduces more variables and requires robots to respond quickly to changing conditions.

“The fault tolerance levels tend to be much lower, but at the same time, the response rates have to be much higher,” Elaprolu said.

AWS is keeping the toolchain hardware-neutral. Rather than prescribing a particular robot, it provides infrastructure for training and deploying models across different machines.

“There’s going to be a wide range of hardware designs and components that are being built and will be built in the future,” Elaprolu said. “The toolchain is intentionally staying neutral to that final step.”

Vulcan is Amazon’s first robot with a sense of touch, using sensors to pick and stow items at a fulfillment center. | Credit: Amazon

Tactile sensing and construction

Elaprolu also pointed to tactile sensing as an example of the specialized capabilities Physical AI may require. AWS has worked with RLWRLD, a South Korean company developing tactile capabilities for humanoid hands. Elaprolu said existing models weren’t sufficiently capable for certain five-finger dexterity tasks, leading AWS and the company to develop a specialized model.

Amazon’s Vulcan robot provides another example. The system uses tactile sensing to help manipulate and stow items in Amazon’s fulfillment centers. The Robot Report recently named Amazon’s Vulcan Robot the 2026 Robot of the Year.

The Toolchain isn’t a tactile-sensing platform, but its support for different data sources, model training, simulation and edge deployment could allow developers to incorporate specialized sensing into their systems.

AWS also sees applications beyond warehouses and factories. Elaprolu pointed to Bedrock Robotics, which has developed hardware and AI models for autonomous construction robots. The models are trained in the cloud on AWS and then used to operate equipment in real construction zones.

An open-source approach

The Physical AI Toolchain is open source, allowing startups and larger companies to use and modify it.

Elaprolu said the individual AWS and NVIDIA components have already been used by customers, including companies participating in AWS’s Physical AI Fellowship with MassRobotics and NVIDIA. The new offering packages those components into a more cohesive workflow.

“It’s the packaging them up and making that seamless for a company that’s going to take forward,” he said.

“We gain substantial scale and resources to accelerate innovation, advance our Intelligent Product Lifecycle vision, and expand our business into more geographies and end markets to serve more customers,” added Neil Barua, president and CEO of PTC.

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

Acquisitions could help Schneider compete with Siemens

The PTC deal could help Schneider Electric compete with Siemens and other global leaders in industrial automation and software in sectors such as aerospace and defense, noted Matthieu Kulezak, a senior analyst at Interact Analysis.

“PTC would extend Schneider’s reach from factory operations and energy management into product design and lifecycle management,” he told The Robot Report. “Together with AVEVA and the proposed Cognite acquisition, it could connect engineering decisions with how products are manufactured, operated and maintained.”

PTC Onshape gives Schneider access to robotics developers and machine-building teams, while PTC‘s Codebeamer supports requirements, testing, and traceability for increasingly complex software-driven products, Kulezak added. “The opportunity is to build relationships earlier, before these customers select automation equipment,” he observed.

Siemens has a lead in simulation capabilities, according to Interact Analysis. PTC may narrow Schneider’s portfolio gap, but it must successfully integrate the technologies of recent acquisitions first.

“Schneider must absorb thousands of employees while aligning product roadmaps, sales incentives, and data architectures,” said Kulezak. “AVEVA’s experience within the group should help, but Schneider will also need to manage adjacent capabilities across AVEVA and Cognite without slowing innovation.”

PTC gives Schneider Electric a shortcut from industrial operations into product engineering, strengthening its challenge to Siemens and Dassault Systèmes. Source: Interact Analysis

Where PTC could deliver

PTC‘s ServiceMax platform for field service could deliver the earliest commercial gains, suggested Kulezak. The connection of product configurations, service histories, and operational data could support maintenance contracts, spare parts, and equipment upgrades. This could produce returns sooner than full integration from engineering to operations, he said.

“Rockwell adds an interesting competitive angle – the company invested $1 billion for approximately 8.4% of PTC in 2018, but sold all its shares by September 2023,” said Kulezak. “Its exit arguably left the door more open to another industrial buyer, although there is no evidence it directly enabled Schneider’s deal. Much of the original partnership centered on [industrial Internet of Things platform] ThingWorx and [IT/OT software] Kepware, which PTC subsequently sold to TPG.”

He cited the stock market reaction as a reflection of both the price and execution risk. Schneider Electric’s shares fell sharply following its announcement.

“The 42.3% premium, substantial financing requirements, and reliance on future synergies likely contributed to investor concerns,” added Kulezak. “In my view, the long-term strategic logic remains compelling; the question is whether Schneider can deliver enough commercial value to justify the price.”

Teradyne Robotics and Elite Robots have reached a mutual agreement resolving a legal dispute over robots and software, bringing the case to an end without either company disclosing the terms of the settlement.

Teradyne Robotics, a subsidiary of Teradyne Inc. and parent company of Universal Robots A/S, announced the settlement on Oct. 1. The resolution aims to bring the dispute between the parties to a close and reflects their shared interest in avoiding the continued time and cost associated with legal proceedings.

Neither company has said what the settlement requires of either side, and there is no public evidence of what Elite Robots agreed to do.

An intellectual property lawyer familiar with this type of litigation, who asked not to be identified and is not involved with the case, told The Robot Report that disputes that begin with an early injunction often end early. The general pattern is that the defendant agrees to stop using the disputed code and pays a fee, but that does not necessarily describe this case.

Inside the dispute

Teradyne Robotics sued Elite Robots Deutschland GmbH earlier this year, alleging copyright infringement involving Universal Robots software. The preliminary injunction was not a final finding of infringement. Elite Robots also did not admit liability as part of the settlement. The companies ultimately agreed to resolve the dispute rather than continue the litigation.

Gen 7 is built around PolyScope X, which Universal Robots described as the software platform for its new generation of robots. PolyScope X includes open APIs and an SDK designed to support AI applications, along with expanded connectivity and programming capabilities.

As the physical world rapidly digitalizes, AI teams are gathering vast amounts of complex video, but transforming raw footage into actionable models remains a critical challenge, according to TwelveLabs Inc. The company today released its Pegasus 1.6 model with added capabilities for understanding and navigating complex real-world environments.

“Our mission has always been to help machines understand how the world works through video,” stated Jae Lee, co-founder and CEO of TwelveLabs. “Physical AI is the next expression of that mission. Most of what people know about doing physical work, such as a changing grip or a recovery after something slips, has never been captured in a form a machine can learn from.”

“With our newest model release, we can now turn that footage into structured, reviewable knowledge, so robotics and physical AI teams can train on real human experience instead of starting from scratch,” he added.

Founded in 2021, TwelveLabs said it has created a “full-stack video intelligence platform” using its Marengo and Pegasus models, which it designed to see and understand video the way humans do in a fraction of the time. Developers can use this single system that gets smarter over time to access and act on all of their video content, said the Seoul-based company.

Pegasus 1.6 focuses on egocentric video

TwelveLabs said its latest version of Pegasus marks its expansion into physical AI, generating rich insights from real-world perspectives. It solves workflow-specific challenges so that machines such as robots, drones, and autonomous vehicles can perceive, reason, and safely act in the physical world like never before, the company claimed.

“We’re focused on the video understanding layer,” Jae Lee told The Robot Report. “You can’t just take millions of hours of video and feed it into a robotics model and expect useful training data to come out. You first need to understand what’s happening in the video, what action is taking place, when it happens, what the person is interacting with, how the behavior changes over time, and when other people or bystanders appear in the field of view.”

“Pegasus 1.6 provides that more precise understanding so robotics and data teams can then turn it into the training data they need,” he added.

TwelveLabs noted that Pegasus 1.6 is its first AI model built to understand egocentric video, which is shot from the point of view of the person doing the work. This could be someone cooking a meal, assembling parts on a factory line, or operating a robot remotely. The model does not require specific cameras, said Lee.

“We’re not requiring robotics teams to use a particular camera or proprietary hardware to capture that footage,” he said. “What matters is being able to capture the actions and interactions taking place from the operator’s point of view.”

In addition, Pegasus 1.6 can work with existing video data and allows for analysis of still images in addition to video.

“One of the reasons we’re focused on egocentric video is that it’s much easier to collect and scale than teleoperation data,” acknowledged Lee. “The goal is to take that footage and make it more useful for robotics teams by identifying the actions taking place, breaking them into precise time segments and capturing finer-grained details about the behavior.”

Head-mounted footage can break models trained on broadcast, instructional, and cinematic video. Source: TwelveLabs

TwelveLabs supports five workflows

Pegasus 1.6 currently supports five workflows powered by its video-native model. They include:

  1. Action segmentation and labeling: This feature accelerates model training with standardized datasets by automatically generating precise, time-stamped action labels for tasks, steps, objects, and hand-object interactions from raw video, mapped to the customer’s domain-specific taxonomy.
  2. Dense caption labeling: This enables natural language understanding for robots by producing rich, descriptive language for spatial relationships, scene context, and hand-object interactions to train advanced language-conditioned robot policies.
  3. Quality scoring: Users can save time by filtering out low-quality video by automatically evaluating and scoring video clips for action clarity, framing, and stability before sending footage to human reviewers.
  4. Search and curation: Customers can uncover critical edge cases by surfacing rare events, long-tail scenarios, and duplicate clips across an entire video repository using simple, natural-language search queries.
  5. Consent and compliance flagging: Privacy and compliance can be maintained by detecting and flagging faces, bystanders, and sensitive onscreen or paper data before video footage enters downstream development pipelines.

]]>

NVIDIA has partnered with Hugging Face to ensure its role in physical AI development. Source: NVIDIA

The physical AI developers determined not to rely on NVIDIA have had some wins lately. OpenAI shipped its own chip. Anthropic stood up an in-house silicon team with salaries that make FAANG recruiters wince.

Also, Advanced Micro Devices acquired World Labs for $8.2 billion, Qualcomm has collaborated with Liquid AI on embedded agents, and Skild AI launched the S1 foundation model. In addition, Google DeepMind integrated Gemini Robotics 2 into Apptronik‘s Apollo 2 humanoid.

And then, almost politely, NVIDIA said it plans to spend $12.9 billion — the biggest acquisition in the company‘s history — buying Hugging Face, the place where the planet’s developers go to pick which model to run. Cute war. NVIDIA just bought the battlefield.

Chasing chips focuses on the wrong layer

Several headlines have read “Labs race to cut NVIDIA loose.” Adorable framing. Here’s the actual scoreboard: While everyone else designed chips, NVIDIA designed an exit ramp that leads straight back to it, no matter which chip wins. That’s not defense. That’s a company that already read the ending and is waiting, patiently, for the rest of the industry to catch up.

The chip numbers are genuinely impressive, to be fair. OpenAI spent nine months with Broadcom on Jalapeño. It is reportedly the fastest tape-out in the history of advanced semiconductors, shipping by year’s end.

Anthropic followed with its own silicon team, posting hardware roles at up to $485,000, stacked on a multi-gigawatt Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) deal it already had running with Google and Broadcom. Google has had TPUs for a decade.

AWS has Trainium. Meta has MTIA. Everyone is racing to stop writing Jensen Huang a check.

None of these very expensive chips touch the place where the other 200,000 companies that will never build their own silicon actually go to find, fine-tune, and ship a model. That layer — the real on-ramp for the rest of the world’s AI adoption — just got quietly annexed by the company everyone claims to be staging a jailbreak from. NVIDIA didn’t flinch; it bought the prison.

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

‘Sovereign’ a clue to NVIDIA’s strategy

Notice the word NVIDIA has kept reaching for in every earnings call so far this year: “sovereigns.” Not developers first. Not enterprises first. Sovereigns — nation-states spending public money on “AI independence” so they’re not permanently on their knees to a handful of U.S. labs.

No government building sovereign AI wants to bet its national compute on OpenAI’s chip, Anthropic’s silicon, or any single lab that might someday become a geopolitical liability. So NVIDIA stepped in with the pitch: “Don’t worry, we’re neutral. Pick any model, any framework, any cloud you like” — a rousing speech about freedom of choice, delivered by the company that just bought the store where all the choices live.

That’s the actual chess move. OpenAI and Anthropic are optimizing their own cost of goods. NVIDIA is optimizing for sitting underneath everyone’s cost of goods, forever, regardless of who wins the fight it’s graciously letting other people have. Nobody at Nvidia will ever put that in an earnings call. They don’t have to. The acquisition makes the argument for them.

Here’s the part nobody wants to say out loud: Even a great custom chip takes years to match the volume, yield, and software maturity of a platform NVIDIA has spent two decades pouring into CUDA.

Jalapeño’s nine-month tape-out is a real engineering flex. But by every account, it’s still a narrow inference chip built for OpenAI’s own workloads — not a platform anyone else is building a business on top of. Anthropic’s silicon team is, charitably, a hiring page with a mission statement, sitting inside a “multi-chip strategy” that still runs mostly on NVIDIA and Google hardware today.

Meanwhile, NVIDIA just bolted on a distribution channel with Hugging Face that gets more daily developer traffic than either lab’s entire platform combined.

NVIDIA says it has the most repos and the second-most homegrown models on Hugging Face. Source: Hugging Face

Sovereign implications get sharper for robotics

The implication gets sharper in physical AI. A robot cannot wait for a distant API to deliberate while it navigates a warehouse, handles sensitive equipment, or makes a safety-critical decision on a factory floor.

It needs local inference, real-time control, sensor data that stays inside the operation, and a deployment stack that does not collapse because a cloud region hiccupped or a vendor changed its terms. That is precisely where “sovereign” stops being a procurement slogan and becomes an operational requirement.

But the same landlord problem follows the robot onto the factory floor. The company that owns the training stack, simulation environment, edge runtime, developer tools, and model marketplace is not merely selling silicon—it is setting the terms for how physical intelligence gets built and deployed.

Physical AI makes hardware choice matter more, not less. It also makes genuine portability across models, compute, and deployment environments far more valuable.

None of this changes much for the companies shipping product to customers — if anything, it sharpens the point. Airrived last month launched its own sovereign AI platform, positioning itself as the agentic OS on a mission to democratize AI and turn every business user into an AI expert.

That’s the other, more literal definition of “sovereign” — not a government hedging its national compute bet on a chip vendor, but a business user who doesn’t need a data center, a silicon roadmap, or a forward-deployed engineer to own and run their AI.

NVIDIA’s version of sovereignty comes with a landlord attached. The application-layer version doesn’t care whose logo is silk-screened onto the silicon underneath it. It cares whether inference is fast, cheap, and boringly reliable, and it is happy to let $2 trillion-adjacent companies fight over who eats the infrastructure bill. That’s the quiet advantage of building lean above the war instead of funding a side in it: The chip fight is enormously expensive to win and completely free to ignore.

Down where the silicon actually gets baked, this isn’t shaping up to be the underdog story the press releases want it to be. OpenAI and Anthropic are spending billions to buy independence from NVIDIA’s hardware. NVIDIA just spent $12.9 billion buying insurance against ever losing either of them — by owning the exact place their models must show up regardless of what chip runs them.

Call it a war if you want. From here, it looks like NVIDIA collecting rent on both sides of the battlefield, smiling, and asking if anyone else would like to diversify.

Anurag Gurtu, co-founder and CEO of Airrived, is an entrepreneur and product leader with more than 20 years of experience across cybersecurity and AI. He has built three generative AI companies, including one that reached unicorn status.

Gurtu is known for turning advanced AI into scalable, real-world platforms, and he previously contributed to successful exits, including acquisitions by Splunk, Tripwire, Sun Microsystems, and FireEye, a public company. He holds an M.S. from the University of Southern California and CISSP certification.

]]> Gaius Capital, a Berlin-based private equity firm focused on business succession in the DACH Mittelstand, has announced the final close of its debut fund, Gaius Nachfolgekapital I, at €50 million.

The oversubscribed fund hit its hard cap alongside an additional €6 million raised through a co-investment vehicle, bringing the total capital secured to €56 million. The final close comes just four months after the fund’s first close at €40 million in June.

]]> Celebrity investment in startups is nothing new, but the range of businesses attracting famous backers is expanding. Beyond traditional endorsements and brand partnerships, celebrities are putting capital into companies working on artificial intelligence, digital healthcare, clean energy, biotechnology and other emerging sectors.

Some are investing directly, while others participate through venture capital firms or dedicated investment vehicles. Their involvement can bring not only funding but also international visibility, industry connections and strategic expertise.

With that in mind, we’ve put together 10 notable celebrity-backed startup deals across Europe. The figures below reflect publicly reported investment amounts, funding rounds or financing arrangements, depending on what has been disclosed. Individual contributions are identified wherever possible.

Kylian Mbappé – Alan (France): €100 million funding round

French football superstar Kylian Mbappé, a World Cup winner and Real Madrid forward, became an investor and ambassador for Paris-based health-tech company Alan in March 2026 through his investment vehicle, Coalition Capital.

Founded in 2016, Alan provides digital health insurance and healthcare services. Earlier that month, the company secured a €100 million funding round, bringing its valuation to approximately €5 billion. It subsequently raised another €480 million in June 2026.

Although Mbappé’s individual investment was not disclosed, he is collaborating with Alan on initiatives related to preventive healthcare, mental health, nutrition and physical activity.

Leonardo DiCaprio – SolarMente (Spain): €50 million financing agreement

American actor and environmental advocate Leonardo DiCaprio, known for films including Titanic, Inception and The Revenant, became an investor in Barcelona-based ClimateTech startup SolarMente in 2024.

Unfortunately for both the founders and Di Caprio’s invesmtent, the company went bankrupt in April of 2026. SolarMente helped households access solar energy through a subscription model that reduces the need for large upfront installation costs.

That has not stopped Leo however, as he has continued his investment trends since then, having this week invested an undisclosed amount in Stockholm-based Energy-as-a-Service company Elvy.

Emma Watson – FabricNano (United Kingdom): €10.5 million Series A

British actress and activist Emma Watson, internationally recognised for playing Hermione Granger in the Harry Potter film series, joined the investors in London-based BioTech startup FabricNano in 2021.

Founded in 2018, FabricNano develops cell-free biomanufacturing technology designed to make industrial production processes more efficient and reduce dependence on fossil fuel-derived materials. Its technology uses immobilised enzymes to support the production of chemicals and other materials.

Pau Gasol – Luzia (Spain): €9.5 million funding round

Spanish basketball legend Pau Gasol, a two-time NBA champion with the Los Angeles Lakers and one of Europe’s most successful basketball players, backed Madrid-based artificial intelligence startup Luzia through his investment vehicle, Gasol16 Ventures.

Luzia develops a generative AI assistant accessible through messaging platforms such as WhatsApp and Telegram, allowing users to interact with artificial intelligence without downloading a separate application.

Elton John – Audoo (United Kingdom): €4.75 million funding round

British singer-songwriter Sir Elton John, whose career spans more than five decades and includes hits such as Rocket Man and Your Song, became an investor in London-based music technology startup Audoo in 2023.

Founded in 2018, Audoo develops audio recognition technology that identifies music played in public places such as shops, restaurants and gyms. Its goal is to provide more accurate data to music rights organisations and help artists receive fairer royalty payments.

Ibai Llanos – Plesh (Spain): €3.75 million funding round

Spanish streamer and entrepreneur Ibai Llanos, known for his massive online audience, the boxing event La Velada del Año and his involvement in the Kings League, entered the FoodTech sector in October 2026.

Together with former Barcelona footballer Gerard Piqué, Llanos led a €3.75 million financing round in Barcelona-based startup Plesh, a company developing chocolate snacks without added sugar.

Snoop Dogg – Sanity Group (Germany): €3 million investment

American rapper and entrepreneur Snoop Dogg, a prominent figure in hip-hop since the 1990s, has developed a broad business portfolio that includes technology and cannabis-related ventures.

Through Casa Verde Capital, the venture capital firm he co-founded, Snoop Dogg is connected an investment in Berlin-based Sanity Group in November 2021.

Founded in 2018, Sanity Group develops products and businesses in medical cannabis and consumer health, combining pharmaceutical expertise with regulated healthcare distribution.

Novak Djokovic – waterdrop (Austria): Seven-figure investment

Serbian tennis champion Novak Djokovic, one of the most successful players in the history of the sport.

In 2023, he became an investor and brand ambassador for Vienna-based startup waterdrop. Founded in 2016, waterdrop develops compact hydration cubes that dissolve in water.

Djokovic made a significant seven-figure investment, according to reports from January 2023. Although the exact figure was not disclosed, his personal commitment represents one of the clearer examples of an individually attributed celebrity investment in a European startup.

Diogo Dalot – Bioniq (United Kingdom): Over €1 million investment

Portuguese professional footballer Diogo Dalot, who plays for Manchester United and the Portuguese national team, joined London-based HealthTech startup Bioniq as an investor in March 2025.

Founded in 2019, Bioniq creates personalised nutritional supplements using blood biomarker data and AI-driven analysis to develop formulations tailored to individual needs.

Dalot contributed over €1 million to the company, joining fellow Portuguese footballer Cristiano Ronaldo, who had invested in Bioniq the previous year.

David Beckham – Guild Esports (United Kingdom): €272k investment

English football icon David Beckham, a former Manchester United and Real Madrid player and one of the world’s most commercially recognisable athletes, entered competitive gaming by investing in London-based Guild Esports in 2020.

Founded in 2019, Guild Esports was established to build professional gaming teams, develop esports talent and compete in international tournaments across major video game titles.

In June 2020, Beckham invested through his business DB Ventures, acquiring shares in the company ahead of its listing on the London Stock Exchange later that year.

Summary

From digital health and AI to biotechnology, solar power and esports, these investments demonstrate how celebrities are becoming participants in Europe’s entrepreneurial ecosystem.

While the amounts and structures vary considerably, the involvement of globally recognised figures can give young companies access to networks, visibility and opportunities that extend beyond traditional startup financing. At the same time, the deals highlight an important distinction: a celebrity’s participation in a multimillion-euro funding round does not necessarily mean that the celebrity invested the full amount personally.

As more athletes, entertainers and creators establish investment vehicles of their own, celebrity-backed startups are likely to remain a visible part of Europe’s innovation landscape.

It is targeting pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies and specialist manufacturers worldwide. While the platform starts with glucose, it is also designed to track other biomarkers, opening the door to continuous sensing far beyond diabetes. 

According to Sava, its microsensors are about ten times shorter than the filament in traditional continuous glucose monitors (CGMs), reducing disruption to the skin while still reaching interstitial fluid. 

The company notes that since the technology was designed from the outset for high-volume manufacture, it is built to reach people at scale. It is now focusing on commercialisation and has therefore partnered with Ascensia to get there at scale.

]]> Ecosia’s decision to drop French AI provider Mistral is not a move towards Chinese technology, but rather a shift towards more affordable, energy-efficient open AI models, founder and CEO Christian Kroll clarified in a conversation with EU-Startups.

“We’ll probably be using Melious.ai in future. Unlike Mistral, this is a European company that offers high-quality, affordable AI inference powered by green electricity,” shared Christian in an exclusive interview.

The Berlin-based search engine recently made headlines after POLITICO reported that it was replacing Mistral with open models, including Chinese offerings such as Alibaba’s Qwen, Z.ai’s GLM and Moonshot AI’s Kimi.

However, Christian stressed that the company’s focus is on open models rather than their country of origin. These offer lower costs, greater flexibility and reduced energy consumption, aligning with Ecosia’s environmental mission.

Addressing concerns about political censorship in Chinese AI models, Christian explained that Ecosia can switch to alternative models when dealing with sensitive subjects, such as questions about Taiwan. The company is also working to eliminate political biases from its AI-generated answers.

The models are accessed through German platform Melious, which operates on European infrastructure powered by low-carbon energy. This allows Ecosia to use internationally developed AI while keeping its infrastructure and data processing in Europe.

“Europe needs its own AI capabilities. At Melious, we run open-weight models on European infrastructure powered by clean energy, outside the reach of the US CLOUD Act. Whether a model was built in Europe, the US or China, it’s simply a set of weights on our servers. It can’t send data back to its makers, and customer data is never retained or used for training. We’re proud to work with Ecosia to show that sovereign AI can deliver strong performance at a fair price,” CEO and co-founder Simon Jakobs told EU-Startups.

Christian also reiterated his concerns about Mistral’s European sovereignty, arguing that its reliance on foreign investors, particularly from the United States, undermines its independence.

This follows a period of significant expansion for Paris-based Mistral AI. In September 2026, the company secured €3 billion in Series D funding, led by Samsung Electronics, at a valuation exceeding €21 billion. The investment followed €722 million in debt financing announced in March to develop its first large-scale data centre near Paris, as well as a €1.7 billion Series C led by Dutch semiconductor equipment manufacturer ASML in September 2025.

Its latest funding round included US investors such as Andreessen Horowitz, Nvidia and Salesforce Ventures, alongside European backers including ASML and Bpifrance. Mistral also participated in a €2.9 million investment in Italian infrastructure startup Clastix.

These come amid wider investment in European AI infrastructure, with financing announcements covered by EU-Startups in 2026 totalling approximately €6.2 billion, including Mistral’s own funding.

Christian contrasted this with Ecosia’s own funding history. The company grew largely without external financing, receiving early backing from German entrepreneur Tim Schumacher. In 2018, Ecosia adopted a steward-ownership structure that prevents the company from being sold or distributing profits to shareholders.

For Ecosia, the switch reflects a broader vision for European technology: rather than depending on individual AI developers, European companies can build competitive, independent services using open models running on European infrastructure.

For Mistral, however, this development implies a loss of trust in what is considered one of Europe’s most promising AI companies.

The startup was founded in 2023 by two ex-Google engineers, Asheem Panakkat, who serves as CEO, and Momchil Ivanov, who serves as CTO. Panikkar spent more than a decade at Google leading teams on Shopping and Lens, while Ivanov worked as a Staff Software Engineer focused on information retrieval. Together, they spotted how the explosion in code being written as large language models became more capable meant the systems used to verify that code were nowhere near ready to keep up.

Their solution: deterministic autonomy. Instead of leaning on large language models to run tests directly, Klarent’s agents use LLMs only to author test code. Once written, the test code executes in a deterministic, repeatable manner, combining the adaptability of AI with the rigour expected in production engineering. There is also a human-in-the-loop verification layer on top, ensuring customers pay only for verified outcomes. 

“At Google, Momo and I could see two things coming at once: LLMs were getting better fast, and the amount of software being created was about to explode. The question that wouldn’t leave us was the feedback loop. How do you keep these coding agents honest? We began by building evals for LLMs and quickly realised the bigger opportunity was QA itself. As AI writes more of the world’s code, testing stops being a cost centre and becomes the thing that determines whether any of that code can be trusted,” said Panakkat.

Their approach has already won over enterprise clients across Europe. JD Sports, Swiss media group NZZ, and mobility company Sixt all use the platform. At JD Sports, Klarent’s AI agents automate multi-system workflows across the e-commerce pipeline, an automation that the retailer said its own teams could not replicate.

The funding will be used by Klarent to support its entry into the United States, building on the momentum seen with its European enterprise customers. The company also plans to grow its engineering team and broaden its cross-platform testing capabilities across web and mobile. It is also pushing into financial services, working with banks and insurance firms where the cost of a broken software release can be catastrophically high.

]]> Besso, a Bern-based startup that helps companies manage the complexity of international trade regulations, has secured €4.29 million (CHF 4 million) in funding.

The funding came from a single large European family office, which opted to remain anonymous. This is a departure from traditional early-stage funding rounds, which have multiple backers, and the company says the funding raised from a single long-term investor was deliberate. 

“We have always been very deliberate about building Besso around real customer demand rather than funding milestones. The traction we are seeing now tells us that the time is right to invest more aggressively in growth. Having one long-term investor take the entire round gives us both the resources and the focus to do exactly that,” said Philip Sieber-Gasser, founder and CEO of Besso.

Founded and headquartered in Bern, Switzerland, Besso helps multinational corporations turn the growing complexity of international trade regulation into a source of competitive advantage. It has built an AI platform that continuously monitors over 1,250 trade regulations and tariff schedules across global corridors, automatically identifying where companies are overpaying on duties and offering them opportunities to recover costs through preferential tariff rates and free trade agreement (FTA) eligibility.

According to the company, global tariff teams miss out on preferential tariff rates on around 30% of eligible shipments. This reportedly costs mid-size importers between $2 million and $15 million annually. In addition to cost, these trade teams are also grappling with more than 7,000 regulatory changes every week across major trade corridors, a figure that has grown due to geopolitics and tariff volatility.

Besso’s AI platform replaces the manual, error-prone processes reliant on spreadsheets, PDFs, and consultancy dependency that most companies currently use to manage their requirements. Besso has already built a strong roster of global clients, including Danone, Unilever, AB-InBev, BASF, Coca-Cola, Heineken, Philip Morris International and Syngenta. The company says additional Fortune 500 companies recently joined the platform.

Alongside its strong client base, the company has built a team with expertise in legal research and is supported by academic partners including the Geneva Graduate Institute, the World Trade Institute, and ETH Zurich. Its advisory board includes Jean-Daniel Gerber, a former Swiss Secretary of State for Economic Affairs, along with other leading trade law academics and AI specialists.

The company, a Venture Leaders alumnus, plans to use the funding to increase its headcount, scale capacity to serve a rapidly growing multinational customer base, and advance its technology platform through continued investment in product development and R&D.

“This is an important milestone for us, but the funding itself is not the destination. What matters is what it enables us to build from here,” added Sieber-Gasser.

With geopolitical uncertainty and shifting tariff regimes reordering the global supply chains, the demand for intelligent trade compliance tools is surging with NMSC forecasting the AI trade compliance market to reach €9.84 billion ($11.05 billion) by 2035, expanding at a 21.07% CAGR. Besso is positioning itself as the platform of record for multinationals looking to reduce trade-related costs and build more resilient supply chains.

<!DOCTYPE html><html lang="en-US"><head><meta charset="UTF-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"><link rel="pingback" href="https://www.studyineurope.eu/xmlrpc.php"> <style id="sie-lean-layout"> #sie-lean-main { margin: 0; }
 #sie-lean-main > *:first-child,
 #sie-lean-main .sie-field-page { margin-top: 0; }

 .et_pb_row_inner { width: 100%; }
 .et_pb_column { position: relative; } </style> <style id="sie-custom-header-inline">/* ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
 SIE Custom Header — v1.1.2
 Zero-CLS, no JavaScript layout shifts.
 No panoramic image — lean 64px nav bar only.
 backdrop-filter is intentionally NOT used on .sie-hdr__bar.
 Any element with backdrop-filter becomes a CSS containing block for
 position:fixed descendants, which would trap the user-ui mobile bottom bar
 (position:fixed; bottom:0) inside the header instead of the viewport.
 ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ */
/* ── Root variables ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
:root {
 --sie-hdr-brand:       #0056b3;        /* SIE brand blue                      */
 --sie-hdr-brand-light: #1a6fc4;
 --sie-hdr-bar-h:       64px;           /* nav bar height — fixed, prevents CLS */
 --sie-hdr-bar-bg:      #0056b3;        /* solid — no backdrop-filter needed   */
 --sie-hdr-bar-border:  rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.15);
}
/* ── Wrapper ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr {
 width: 100%;
 display: block;
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 /* Own stacking context so dropdowns render above Divi page content */
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1000;
}
/* ── Navigation bar ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__bar {
 height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter here — it would trap position:fixed children
 (user-ui mobile bottom bar) inside this element instead of viewport */
 border-bottom: 1px solid var(--sie-hdr-bar-border);
}
.sie-hdr__inner {
 max-width: 1280px;
 height: 100%;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 32px;
}
/* ── Logo ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__logo {
 flex-shrink: 0;
 text-decoration: none;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-img {
 height: 54px;
 width: auto;
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-text {
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 17px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: #fff;
 letter-spacing: -0.01em;
 white-space: nowrap;
}
/* ── Desktop navigation ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__nav {
 flex: 1;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list {
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list li {
 position: relative;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 padding: 8px 14px;
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 text-decoration: none;
 border-radius: 8px;
 transition: background 0.15s ease, color 0.15s ease;
 white-space: nowrap;
 min-height: 48px; /* WCAG touch target */
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a:hover,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle:hover,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 color: #fff;
}
/* ── Resources dropdown ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: none;
 position: absolute;
 top: calc(100% + 6px);
 left: 0;
 min-width: 240px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 12px;
 box-shadow: 0 12px 40px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.18);
 padding: 8px 0;
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 z-index: 9999;
}
/* CSS-only hover on desktop */
@media (hover: hover) {
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown,
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:focus-within > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
 }
}
/* JS-toggled state (mobile / keyboard) */
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown li {
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a {
 display: block;
 padding: 10px 18px;
 font-size: 13.5px;
 color: #003B73;
 font-weight: 500;
 border-radius: 0;
 min-height: unset;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a:hover {
 background: #f0f7ff;
 color: #0b5394;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transition: transform 0.2s ease;
}
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transform: rotate(180deg);
}
/* ── Mobile hamburger ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: none;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: center;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 5px;
 width: 44px;
 height: 44px;
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 0;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger span {
 display: block;
 width: 22px;
 height: 2px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 2px;
 transition: transform 0.25s ease, opacity 0.25s ease;
}
/* Animate to ✕ when open */
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(1) {
 transform: translateY(7px) rotate(45deg);
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(2) {
 opacity: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(3) {
 transform: translateY(-7px) rotate(-45deg);
}
/* ── User-UI icon bar integration ────────────────────────────────────────────
 user-ui.php's desktop bar uses position:absolute; top:20px; right:30px — that
 was designed for Divi's header context. Inside our flex .sie-hdr__inner we
 need it as a normal flex child instead.
 Fixed-position children (auth drawer, mobile bar, destinations panel) are
 unaffected — position:fixed is always viewport-relative provided no ancestor
 has backdrop-filter, transform, or perspective (we intentionally avoid all
 three on .sie-hdr__bar).
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 position: static !important;
 top: auto !important;
 right: auto !important;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
/* Align our mobile breakpoint (860px) with user-ui's desktop/mobile split */
@media (min-width: 861px) {
 .sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 display: flex !important;
 }
}
@media (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 display: none !important;
 }
}
/* Leonardo icon in the nav bar.
 user-ui's default .se-ai-icon is 86×86 px (fine for the mobile bottom bar),
 but that overflows our 64px-tall nav bar. Override to a crisp 36px square —
 the webp source is already high-res so it stays sharp at 2× on retina. */
.sie-hdr .se-ai-icon {
 width:  36px !important;
 height: 36px !important;
 border-radius: 50%;
 object-fit: cover;
}
/* Icon colours inside the header.
 user-ui defaults: map icon is #2f6fed (dark blue) and heart is #F44336 (red).
 The map icon is nearly invisible on our #0056b3 bar — lift all icons to white.
 The heart keeps its red via the !important below so favourited items still pop. */
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon {
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.85) !important;
}
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon:hover {
 color: #fff !important;
}
/* Fav heart — keep the red so it reads as "save" */
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link {
 color: #ff6b6b !important;   /* slightly lighter red, readable on blue */
}
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link:hover {
 color: #ff4444 !important;
}
/* ── Responsive ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
@media (max-width: 860px) {
 :root {
 --sie-hdr-bar-h: 56px;
 }
 .sie-hdr {
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 }
 .sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: flex;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav {
 /* Hidden off-screen when closed — no layout shift */
 position: absolute;
 top: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);           /* flush below the nav bar */
 left: 0;
 right: 0;
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter — same reason as .sie-hdr__bar */
 padding: 12px 0 20px;
 clip-path: inset(0 0 100% 0);       /* collapses upward — no CLS */
 transition: clip-path 0.3s ease;
 z-index: 9998;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav.is-open {
 clip-path: inset(0);
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav-list {
 flex-direction: column;
 align-items: flex-start;
 gap: 0;
 padding: 0 16px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav-list a,
 .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 width: 100%;
 font-size: 15px;
 padding: 12px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 position: static;
 box-shadow: none;
 border-radius: 0;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.06);
 padding: 4px 0 4px 16px;
 margin: 4px 0;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown a {
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.8);
 font-size: 14px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown a:hover {
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.08);
 color: #fff;
 }
}
@media (max-width: 480px) {
 .sie-hdr__inner {
 padding: 0 16px;
 gap: 16px;
 }
}
/* Hover-gap fix: invisible bridge spanning the 6px gap between the nav item
 and the dropdown panel, so the cursor never "leaves" while crossing. */
.sie-hdr__dropdown::before {
 content: "";
 position: absolute;
 top: -10px;
 left: 0;
 right: 0;
 height: 10px;
}

.sie-dest-panel,
#sie-auth-drawer,
#sie-lead-form-drawer,
.sie-finder-overlay {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;

 DESTINATIONS PANEL  — overlay + grid
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
 /* Outer layer: covers full viewport */
 .sie-dest-panel {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 2147483000;
 display: flex;
 align-items: stretch;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;
 pointer-events: none;
 transition: opacity .25s ease, visibility .25s;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open {
 opacity: 1;
 visibility: visible;
 pointer-events: auto;
 }
 /* Backdrop */
 .sie-dest-panel__backdrop {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 background: rgba(11, 55, 112, .52);
 backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 cursor: pointer;
 }
 /* Sheet — right-panel on desktop */
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1;
 width: min(800px, 100%);
 height: 100%;
 background: #fff;
 overflow-y: auto;
 -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch;
 padding: 26px 26px 40px;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 gap: 0;
 transform: translateX(28px);
 opacity: 0;
 transition: transform .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1), opacity .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1);
 box-shadow: -20px 0 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateX(0);
 opacity: 1;
 }
 /* Mobile: bottom-sheet */
 @media (max-width: 767px) {
 .sie-dest-panel {
 align-items: flex-end;
 justify-content: stretch;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 width: 100%;
 height: 92vh;
 border-top-left-radius: 22px;
 border-top-right-radius: 22px;
 padding: 20px 16px 40px;
 transform: translateY(28px);
 box-shadow: 0 -16px 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateY(0);
 }
 }
 /* ── Header ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__header {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 justify-content: space-between;
 margin-bottom: 6px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__titlewrap {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 10px;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__globe {
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #1e66f5;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__title {
 font-size: 1.5rem;
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #0b3770;
 margin: 0;
 line-height: 1.2;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close {
 background: transparent;
 border: 0;
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #0b3770;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 6px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 line-height: 1;
 opacity: .75;
 transition: opacity .15s, background .15s;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close:hover {
 opacity: 1;
 background: #f0f4ff;
 }
 /* Subheading */
 .sie-dest-panel__sub {
 color: #466087;
 font-size: .94rem;
 margin: 0 0 20px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 /* ── Country grid ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 display: grid;
 grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr);
 gap: 14px;
 /* allow this to grow and scroll */
 flex: 1;
 align-content: start;
 }
 @media (max-width: 620px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr);
 gap: 10px;
 }
 }
 @media (min-width: 621px) and (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
 }
 }
 /* ── Country card ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__card {
 position: relative;
 display: block;
 aspect-ratio: 3 / 2;
 border-radius: 12px;
 overflow: hidden;
 text-decoration: none;
 background: #1d3557;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card--no-img .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 background: linear-gradient(135deg, #1d3557 0%, #1e66f5 100%);
 }
 /* Hero image layer — scales on hover */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 transition: transform .4s ease;
 will-change: transform;
 }
 /* <img> fills the card exactly like background-size:cover did.
 loading="lazy" means the browser only fetches each image when the
 panel opens and the card enters the viewport — saving ~30 MB of
 upfront image requests on every page that includes this panel. */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-img {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center;
 display: block;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-bg,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 transform: scale(1.07);
 }
 /* Gradient overlay + text */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-body {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 padding: 10px 12px 10px;
 background: linear-gradient(
 to top,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .72) 0%,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .30) 55%,
 transparent 100%
 );
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card-name {
 color: #fff;
 font-weight: 700;
 font-size: .92rem;
 line-height: 1.2;
 text-shadow: 0 1px 5px rgba(0,0,0,.55);
 display: block;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {
 display: block;
 color: rgba(255,255,255,0);
 font-size: .75rem;
 margin-top: 2px;
 transition: color .2s ease, transform .2s ease;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {
 color: rgba(255,255,255,.9);
 transform: translateX(4px);
 }
 /* ── Body-scroll lock ── */
 body.sie-dest-panel-open {
 overflow: hidden;
 }
 /* ── Country interest heart ── */
 .sie-country-heart {
 position: absolute;
 top: 8px;
 right: 8px;
 z-index: 10;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 border: none;
 border-radius: 20px;
 padding: 4px 8px 4px 7px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 cursor: pointer;
 font-size: 13px;
 color: #94a3b8;
 box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.22);
 backdrop-filter: blur(6px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(6px);
 transition: color .18s, transform .18s, background .18s;
 line-height: 1;
 min-width: 28px;
 justify-content: center;
 }
 .sie-country-heart:hover {
 transform: scale(1.12);
 background: #fff;
 color: #ef4444;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.voted {
 color: #ef4444;
 background: #fff;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.voted i {
 animation: sie-heart-pop .35s cubic-bezier(.36,.07,.19,.97);
 }
 @keyframes sie-heart-pop {
 0%   { transform: scale(1); }
 40%  { transform: scale(1.45); }
 70%  { transform: scale(.88); }
 100% { transform: scale(1); }
 }
 .sie-country-heart__count {
 font-size: 11px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: inherit;
 display: none;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.has-votes .sie-country-heart__count {
 display: inline;
 }
 /* ── Trigger button styles (for use in any menu) ── */
 /* Desktop globe icon */
 .se-dest-desktop-btn {
 font-size: 24px;
 color: #fff;
 text-decoration: none;
 cursor: pointer;
 transition: transform .2s, color .2s;
 position: relative;
 line-height: 1;
 background: transparent;
 border: 0;
 padding: 0;
 }
 .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover {
 transform: scale(1.15);
 color: #FFCC00;
 }
 /* Tooltip on desktop */
 @media (min-width: 1024px) {
 .se-dest-desktop-btn::after {
 content: "Study Destinations";
 position: absolute;
 bottom: -30px;
 left: 50%;
 transform: translateX(-50%);
 background: #007BFF;
 color: #fff;
 padding: 4px 8px;
 font-size: 12px;
 border-radius: 5px;
 opacity: 0;
 pointer-events: none;
 transition: opacity .2s;
 white-space: nowrap;
 }
 .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover::after {
 opacity: 1;
 }
 }
 /* Mobile pill button */
 .se-dest-btn {
 background: #0b3770 !important;
 color: #fff !important;
 }
 .se-dest-btn:hover {
 background: #1e66f5 !important;

<span><span>sandoel</span></span>

<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2><strong>How does the Conference work?</strong></h2>

<p>Europeans can share ideas via the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Multilingual Digital Platform</a>, and both national and&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/assemblies/citizens-panels" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">European Citizens' Panels</a>. These contributions feed into the&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/plenary" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference Plenaries</a>.</p>

<p>The Conference&nbsp;offers a new public forum for an open, inclusive, and transparent debate with citizens around a number of key priorities and challenges.</p>

<h2><strong>How can you participate?</strong></h2>

<ul>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]--><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/processes?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">share your own ideas or support others’ ideas</a> on the multilingual digital Conference platform</li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->organise your own events and promote it by adding them to the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference platform</a></li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->take a look at the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/meetings" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">events organised by people across the EU</a></li>
</ul>

<h2><strong>What will the outcome be?</strong></h2>

<p>All of the ideas gathered and reports on events are published on the platform openly and transparently. These reports will then directly influence the discussions in the European Citizens’ Panels as well as in the Plenaries, where citizens will enter into a dialogue with national and European decision makers.</p>

<p>By spring 2022, the Conference will provide guidance on the future of Europe to the European institutions</p>

<p><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/getinvolved" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Get involved and make your voice heard when it comes to education, culture, youth, sport, and more</a>.</p>

<p>Follow on Twitter at&nbsp;</p>

<ul>

</ul>

<h1 class="title-h1 eac-page-title">European Student Card Initiative at EAIE 2026 in Glasgow - main highlights</h1>
<span><span>holbobe</span></span>
<span><time datetime="2026-09-30T09:11:45+02:00" title="Wednesday, September 30, 2026 - 09:11">Wed, 09/30/2026 - 09:11</time>
</span>
<div class="ecl"><p>EAIE 2026 took place from 8 to 11 September, with this year’s theme being “The Rhythm of Revolution”. ESCI featured in five activities: two sessions in the main conference programme and three mini-sessions at the European Commission stand.</p><h2>Shaping the next phase of the ESCI</h2><p>The session “What’s next for the European Student Card Initiative?” brought together Victor Aguilar Mendez from the European Commission, Harpa Sif Arnarsdóttir from RANNIS and Sergi Martínez Rigol from the University of Barcelona to discuss the roadmap beyond 2027.</p><p>The discussion highlighted three main points:</p><ul><li data-list-item-id="ec04a08fab5a0a15faf6d0537ff166c1e"><strong>Build on strong foundations</strong>. Participants welcomed the ambition to further simplify student mobility and emphasised the importance of building on the progress already achieved. They also noted that digital transformation involves more than technical connections, requiring aligned processes, staff capacity and resources.</li><li data-list-item-id="ec8f6683d0b4c64c36760e88ede263ada"><strong>Give institutions clarity and time to prepare</strong>. Participants highlighted the value of clear information on the <a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/european-student-card-initiative/about/esci-2028-2034/continuity-and-preparation?">future scope of ESCI+</a>, practical implications and transition arrangements. The European Commission indicated that 2028 and 2029 are envisaged as transition years.</li><li data-list-item-id="e8a2629faf233a9053a3e7c84c25e2248"><strong>Broaden engagement beyond international relations and IT teams</strong>. Participants highlighted the value of involving university leadership, national authorities, governance bodies and research and education networks.</li></ul><h2>Practical exchange at the European Commission stand</h2><p>Three mini-sessions created space for practical discussion and peer exchange at the European Commission stand:</p><ul><li data-list-item-id="ea46800eaa0963f636bf8742a636fe844"><strong>Digital Officers and ESCI Champions</strong>: “Meet and Greet” explored different opportunities for close collaboration and participants discussed faster communication channels, technical sub-groups and ways to strengthen the community of practitioners.</li><li data-list-item-id="e722608eb7be29071793748afb04db370"><strong>ESCI+ timeline: what to expect and when</strong>, focused on preparations in 2026 and plans for 2027. Participants asked for timely communication, hands-on training, transition arrangements and support to integrate future developments with existing systems.</li><li data-list-item-id="e4abeb75d22c4e87d628dd3a9174bdc0a"><strong>How to issue your first European Student Card</strong> introduced the practical tools available to card issuers, including the ESC Router and the ESC Service Manager for listing services available to ESC holders.</li></ul><h2>Poster session: “The European Student Card: Bridging borders for students”</h2><p>The poster attracted strong interest, with ESCI representatives Elodie Ham (EACEA) and Deborah Arnold (NTT DATA) engaging with participants on the ESCI components and discussing the implications of the ESCI+ timeline with those already involved in the initiative as well as with potential newcomers.</p><h2>Session by ESCI Champions: “Erasmus Without Paper: Getting on board with the digitisation of Erasmus+"&nbsp;</h2></div>
<div class="ecl-u-type-bold ecl-u-mb-m">Intro Text</div><div class="eac-hero"><p>We joined more than 7,300 international education professionals from over 100 countries in Glasgow to discuss what comes next for the European Student Card Initiative and share practical guidance with institutions.</p></div>

  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2>Looking ahead</h2><p>Preparation for ESCI+ will continue in close dialogue with all stakeholders via support and user training planned for 2027, helping institutions build on existing progress and prepare for the next phase at a sustainable pace.</p><p>The discussions in Glasgow demonstrated a shared commitment to making student mobility simpler, more connected and more accessible.                         <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has a strategy and an overarching structure supporting internationalisation</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>

                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The internationalisation strategy is available and prominently displayed on your website</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Internationalisation is an important driver for institutional change, and has a great influence on the major activities of a higher education institution (HEI) i.e. education and research. The importance of internationalisation is recognised, and most institutions have a strategy for internationalisation. However, for a strategy to be efficient, and for it to drive the HEI's activities regarding internationalisation, there is a need for its acceptance from across the whole institution. In addition the strategy could also be accessible to external collaborative partners. It is highly important to have the institution's internationalisation and modernisation strategy published and easily accessible to all.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The institution has a clear plan to implement the strategy</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The strategy and policy should include explicit allocation of responsibilities for its efficient implementation to individuals at all levels of the institution, from senior management to the heads of departments, schools and faculties, to academic and administrative staff. This will ensure acceptance and accountability for the strategy. The internationalisation strategy and policy should outline a specific implementation plan that sets out explicitly the financial and human resources available.&nbsp; For example, it is recommended to set up an International Relations Office (IRO) to implement mobility and other international projects.</p><p>As with any other activity, the institutional implementation of the internationalisation strategy is dependent on the people behind the activities. It is highly important for an institution to have staff with the right set of skills and knowledge driving the internationalisation agenda and liaising with international students and staff members. Therefore understanding the development needs of the staff and supporting their professional development should be a high priority for the institution. Such development should focus on both staff engaged in international activities as well as the supporting staff, ensuring the most efficient implementation of international activities and cooperative projects across the institution. For example, trainings/webinars/projects could be organised on intercultural competences and communication, project management, enhancement of internationalisation at home/intercultural, or other activities suggested by the staff and supported by the hierarchy.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes incoming and outgoing student and staff mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Mobility is important to the development of the institution as a whole as well as for the individual participants. Therefore the HEI should make mobility and international cooperation a central element in its institutional policies, and explicitly and consistently promote and support student and staff mobility. Non-discrimination policies and further emphasis on the promotion of mobility for under-represented groups should also form an integral part of the institutional support structures.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes engagement in European and international cooperation projects</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution's internationalisation strategy and policy should explicitly and consistently promote the development of cooperation with partners in other EU and non-EU countries. The activities and co-operation projects agreed by the HEI should be based on identified needs. In addition they should identify geographical and subject priorities of the internationalisation strategy.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The implementation of the strategic plan is monitored</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>International activity, including co-operation projects and mobility should be carefully monitored. Clear and unambiguous monitoring of such activity are key to ensuring success. Explicit indicators should be developed to show specific success scenarios. The indicators should be SMART.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Incentives are provided to staff involved in international activities</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Participation in such international projects should be seen as an important aspect of the professional development of the staff and of the modernisation of the HEI. It should, therefore, be considered a key component in staff evaluation.                          <p>In signing the Erasmus Charter for Higher Education, the institution agrees to respect <strong>in full</strong> the principles of non-discrimination as set out in the Programme.                                                 <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Ensuring that the mobile participant, sending and receiving HEI/organisation/enterprise (i.e. all three parties) sign the Learning Agreement before the start of the mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The purpose of the Learning Agreement is to provide a transparent and efficient preparation of the study period abroad and to ensure that the student will receive recognition in his/her degree for the educational components or traineeship successfully completed abroad. The Learning Agreement:</p><ul><li>Sets out the learning outcomes for the mobility, including both the educational components or traineeship activities to be carried out by the student at the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise, which will be recognised by the sending institution upon successful completion of the study programme abroad and counted towards his/her degree.</li><li>Ensures full recognition for satisfactorily completed activities of study mobility and traineeships in terms of credits awarded, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams, and documents these credits in the student records, so that they can be identified in a transparent way.</li></ul><p>The Learning Agreement is binding for all parties and constitutes the cornerstone of successful student mobility (for studies, traineeships, and combinations thereof), including quality assurances and the process for transparent transfer of credits. Therefore, it is essential to conduct mobility based on an agreed and signed Learning Agreement. The Learning Agreement should be agreed and signed by all parties (the student, the sending institution and the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise) before the start of the mobility. It is not compulsory to circulate papers with original signatures; scanned copies of signatures or digital signatures may be accepted, depending on the national legislation.</p><p>The EU official templates for Learning Agreements for studies and traineeships are available online: <a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm&nbsp;&nbsp;</a></p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Including allocation of responsibility to an academic who has the authority to approve, amend and recognise the Learning Agreements on behalf of the responsible academic body</span>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has established formal procedures for recognising staff mobility for both teaching and training activities abroad</div>

                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Ensuring that the mobile participant, sending and receiving institution/organisation/enterprise (i.e. all three parties) sign the mobility agreement before the start of the mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>To ensure effective staff mobility, it has to be based on a signed mobility agreement. The mobility agreement has to acceptable and signed by all parties in advance. There are four key elements set out by the mobility agreement, which are intended to increase the relevance and potential impact of the mobility. These are:</p><ul><li>The overall objectives and academic rationale of the mobility,</li><li>The institutional requirements or strategy, and the mobility's added value in the context of modernisation and internationalisation,</li><li>The activities or teaching programme content to be undertaken by the staff member, and,</li><li>The expected outcomes and impact of the mobility on the professional development of the staff member at both institutions.</li></ul><p>For this to work effectively, there needs to be dialogue and discussion between the three parties prior to the signing of the mobility agreement having agreed the common goals which are acceptable.&nbsp;</p>                      </div>

        <h2 class="eche-report-section-title eche-pdf-page-break">During the mobility</h2>
        <div class="eche-report-section-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-report-full-question-wrapper">
                <div class="eche-officer-question-title-wrapper">
                    <div class="eche-report-title-icons-wrapper">

                            <div class="eche-report-officer-number-text">10</div>
                        </div>
                        <div class="eche-officer-question-icon"><img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/ECHE__OFFICERS_Q10.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">
</div>
